headline: Activists in Huelva oppose the expansion of Enagás’ LNG infrastructure, arguing that investments in liquefied natural gas projects reinforce fossil-fuel dependence while worsening local environmental and social impacts.
description: Enagás (acronym for Empresa Nacional del Gas), the Spanish gas transmission network operator  [6] [7]   [11] . In May 2022, the company announced a potential increase in the liquified natural gas (LNG) shipments due to the growing energy tension unravelled by the war in Ukraine [2] . Huelva is home to the Polo Químico, one of the main industrial complexes in Southern Europe, where the chemical, energy and petrochemical industries are concentrated, including Enagás’ LNG regasification plant  [1]   [2] . Enagás aims to expand the Huelva plant to become “one of the most important regasification plants in Spain” according to the Port of Huelva’s director  [2] . Currently the plant has five storage tanks with a total capacity of 619,500 m³ of LNG  [12]   [13] . This capacity allows it to have a regasification capacity of up to 1,350,000 m³/hour, which is the maximum volume of gas it can convert from liquid to gas per hour  [12]    [13] . Environmental and Societal Impacts The province of Huelva is “one of the worst affected in Europe by the dynamics of its chemical and gas industries, which have been a source of danger and unhealthiness for its inhabitants for decades”  [2] . Phosphogypsum ponds, radioactive waste, and the release of industrial pollutants into the atmosphere have been harming the health of local populations and ecosystems for years  [3]   [4] . This is due to the fact that the area has become a hub of highly toxic industrial and mining sectors which have contaminated the entire surrounding area and public institutions instead of addressing the issue continue to promote such industries  [2] . The Enagás facilities with the regasification plant, storage tanks and gigantic LNG carriers in the Port of Huelva accelerates the dangers that the energy and chemical industry poses to the area, its population and the natural environment  [1] . Numerous civil society groups have been demanding an end to the production and consumption model based on fossil fuels, which has systematically violated human rights and accelerated climate change  [3]   [4] . The growing international gas prices put large segments of society at risk, and unravelled a much more severe energy crisis in the Global South  [3]   [4] . Rebelión por el Clima (Climate Rebellion) also points out that 78% of the gas consumed in Spain is used by industries and electricity generation  [3]   [4] . In Andalucia this figure is even bigger, 84.6% with Huelva and Cádiz being the provinces with the highest rates  [3]   [4] . In contrast, families experience energy poverty due to the soaring prices and inflation  [3]   [4] . Therefore Rebelión por el Clima (Climate Rebellion) demands the dismantling of these infrastructures and the establishment of renewable energy and energy conservation practices including conversion to renewable heating, self-consumption systems and improving insulation by 2035  [3]   [4] . Resistance Around September 2022, a protest by Ecologistas en Acción (Ecologists in Action) gathered at the Juan Carlos I pier, which is opposite to the gas facilities at the port of Huelva  [1] . The organisation demanded a stop to fossil fuel companies and greenwashing  [1] . Following, in October the same year around a hundred activists from the Rebelión por el Clima (Climate Rebellion) movement (of which Ecologistas en Acción (Ecologists in Action) is part of) blocked the headquarters of Enagás at the Huelva Chemical Complex  [2]   [5] . The group used the slogan “Families are freezing while their future burns here” criticising the company and shedding light that the most vulnerable people are suffering due to the price surge and the climate crisis  [2] . They have also highlighted the inadequacy of the Plan Más Seguridad Energética (More Energy Security Plan), approved on October 11 by the Government, which has been heavily influenced by industrial corporations and binds citizens on fossil fuel dependence  [2] . Expansion of the project Despite the protests in 2022, the LNG terminal in Huelva has continued to expand. In 2023, Alberto Santana, President of the Port of Huelva, and Arturo Gonzalo, CEO of Enagás, signed a protocol to explore innovation opportunities related to renewable gases such as hydrogen and Bio-LNG [8] . During the same period, LNG bunkering activity increased significantly, with the company quadrupling fuel supply to ships between 2021 and 2023 [9] . Operational activity also continued to grow. In 2024, the Huelva terminal received 38 LNG carriers and unloaded more than 5 million m³ of LNG. That same year, the facility obtained authorization to upgrade its mooring system to accommodate vessels of up to 180,000 m³, allowing it to receive larger methane carriers and reinforcing its role as one of Spain’s major LNG terminals [10] .

headline: Sustained protests, guerrilla campaigns, policy advocacy, and financial pressure halted an LNG terminal in Bratislava.
description: In Bratislava, Slovakia, the state-owned investor Public Ports company Verejné Prístavy proposed the construction of a liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal on the Danube, with an expected lifespan of 20 to 40 years  [1]   [18] . Following a planned environmental impact assessment study, construction of the new terminal was supposed to begin in 2022 and end in 2026, with an estimated cost of approximately 40 million euros  [17]   [18] . The port would cover 5,500 square meters on the Pálenisko port peninsula and would be located in close proximity to the city centre, just a short distance from a cycle path, a gardening area, and the Žitný ostrov Nature Reserve, which is the largest source of drinking water in Central Europe  [1]   [17]   [18] .. The terminal would be used to refuel road tankers, provide LNG storage, and serve as a bunkering facility for ships  [17]   [20] . It would involve storage tanks, technological equipment to maintain the fuel at low temperatures, and a dispensing point for pumping fuel into ship tanks, classifying it as a small-scale LNG bunkering facility  [20] . The company claims that the project would introduce alternative fuels and reduce greenhouse gas emissions as part of the EU plan to develop the Rhine–Danube transport corridor  [17]  . Environmental Impacts However, Greenpeace Slovakia claims that the plan to build an LNG terminal in Bratislava is outdated and does not take into account the latest developments of climate change mitigation plans, as currently wind and solar are the cheapest forms of energy supply in most major markets  [1] . The claim that the LNG terminal reduces greenhouse gas emissions is a fallacy, as considering the entire life cycle, it does not reduce emissions compared to conventional fuels  [1] . Natural gas is 80% methane, a greenhouse gas that has up to 82.5 times the global warming potential of CO2 over a 20-year period  [1] . Furthermore, Transport & Environment has calculated that uncontrolled methane leakage may even increase emissions from shipping  [1] . Establishing a new LNG plant would accelerate climate change, which has already resulted in some places in Slovakia up to 50% reduction in water resources, devastating droughts lasting several years or increasingly intense torrential rains  [1] . Additionally, an LNG terminal would pose a severe safety risk for the city centre and residential areas, as LNG is a highly flammable substance, and over the past 30 years, more than 19 LNG accidents have been documented  [1] . It can potentially worsen the city’s air quality as it increases freight traffic density  [1] . Moreover, while LNG tanks have a double-walled structure with thermal insulation layers making leakage unlikely, pollution can occur from other chemicals used, such as in the storage and transportation of LNG (corrosion inhibitors, coolants, cleaning agents, emulsion agents, various additives), which can impact the Natural Reserve waters  [1] .  Greenpeace Slovakia claims that a report analysing 104 LNG-related accidents between 1944 and 2024 highlights that areas within a two-kilometre radius of LNG facilities face the highest risk [15] . In the case of Bratislava, this zone includes densely populated areas such as Eurovea, Mlynské Nivy, and Ovsište in Petržalka, as well as the Slovnaft refinery located only 1.5 km from the proposed terminal, which could amplify accident-related impacts  [15] . The report warns that risks such as vapour cloud explosions, pool fires, and jet fires may be underestimated by the industry by a factor of 15 to 20, posing serious threats to nearby populations and infrastructure  [15] . These risks are further intensified by climate-related extreme events, as the planned terminal site was flooded during recent floods, raising concerns about the facility’s resilience and environmental safety  [15] . Resistance tactics The civil society in Bratislava has employed a wide variety of tactics against the proposed LNG facilities. In 2021 June, on the day of the hearings of the LNG plans, Greenpeace protested in front of the Ministry of Transport; furthermore, together with other partners, the organisation submitted allegations against the Environmental Impact Assessment  [2] . In the same year, they have also put out guerrilla campaigns all around the city, advertisements about “greenwashing” by gas companies and posters in local restaurants with a link to sign and oppose fossil fuels  [3]   [4] . Greenpeace also established an infostand around the city weekly, and organisers on bikes and kayaks went around the city with short infomercials about the terminal  [5]   [6]   [8] . There were also collaborations with influencers and content creators, spreading information about the proposed LNG plans and their impacts  [10]   [11] . Greenpeace, in collaboration with expert James Turitt from the Clean Air Task Force, monitored methane emissions from gas infrastructures in Slovakia through an infrared camera [7] . In total, 31 cases of methane emissions were documented at seven locations, four compressor stations in Veľké Kapušany, Veľké Zlievece, Ivanka pri Nitre and Lakšárská Nová Ves, an underground gas storage facility in Plavecký Štvrtek, a national transfer station in Špačince and an SPP Distribution control station near Lozorno  [7] . Greenpeace held advocacy meetings with the City Hall and the Mayor of the city district, which was in close proximity to the planned terminal. Furthermore, they had a lobbying meeting with the Ministry of Transportation. Activists from Friends of the Earth-CEPA, From Benches to Streets, Turning Point, Concerned Mothers, Extinction Rebellion and Greenpeace Slovakia, before the discussion of the Bratislava Public Port Development Strategy, symbolically expressed their opposition to the construction of an LNG terminal in Bratislava  [12] . Greenpeace Slovakia have also disrupted the Central European Energy Conference during the initial discussion on increasing energy security with a banner stating “gas = energy crisis”  [1]   [9] . Just a short distance from the conference, a second 20-meter banner was hung outside of the MR Štefánik Square in Bratislava by activists from Slovakia, Poland, Croatia, Austria and Hungary, which drew attention to energy security with renewable resources, not oil, natural gas or coal  [1]   [9] . A Greenpeace activist, Katarína Juríková, stated that the energy crisis will not be solved by “replacing one gas supplier with another”, rather “investment should go into renewable energy sources (...) with a sufficient financial support for people so that everyone can afford these changes”  [9] . Moreover, Greenpeace Slovakia, Friends of Earth - CEPA, Concerned Mothers and From the Benches to the Streets launched a public appeal for residents to express their opposition to the planned construction of the LNG terminal [13]   [21] . Yet, the Ministry of Environment rejected the appeal, arguing that the terminal would not be in conflict with the Paris Agreement and that the transition to low-emission alternatives in river transport is not realistic in the near future [14] . The Ministry also stated that methane leaks, which can have an impact during construction and operation, need to be addressed at a global level  [14] . In contrast, Greenpeace stated regarding low-emission alternative technologies that “His argument is in direct contradiction with the conclusions of the European Parliament and the Council, which state in the proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on the deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure and repealing Directive 2014/94/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council that “unlike maritime transport, in inland waterway transport, where smaller vessels are commonly used and cover shorter distances, zero-emission propulsion technologies such as hydrogen and electricity should enter the market more quickly. LNG is not expected to play a significant role in this sector anymore.”   [14] . The contract governing the provision of a non-refundable financial contribution stipulates that the state-owned joint-stock company, Verejné prístavy, must take out insurance [16] . Therefore, insurance companies such as Allianz, Kooperative, Komunálna poisťovňa, Uniqua, Generali, Union, Collonade, ČSOB, and Wüstenrot received letters from Greenpeace Slovakia asking them not to insure the planned LNG terminal, as the company then would not fulfil the obligation and would have to return the funds obtained  [16] . Success As of 2026, the LNG terminal in Bratislava was cancelled, and the Public Ports stated, “The project plan is in the phase of completed pre-project preparation, specifically at the level of processing the feasibility study and related analytical and evaluation documents […]. The LNG terminal project in the Port of Bratislava has not yet been approved or has a valid implementation schedule. After the completion of the pre-project preparation, a decision was not made to transition the project to the implementation phase. The project is currently not being implemented,” [19] . Greenpeace stated that the cancellation was mainly due to financial and strategic reasons, as the terminal did not receive support under the AFIF (Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Facility, which is an EU financial instrument for alternative fuels in transport) call, as it was primarily focused on infrastructure for low-emission and zero-emission technologies  [19]   [20] . The organisation also stated that this decision has been impacted by the fact that the current demand for LNG as a fuel for inland waterway support on the Danube is limited and that out of the three projects planned (two in Bratislava, one in Komárno), none was implemented (19). Without enough customers, the terminal would not have been stable economically  [20] . Yet, even with successful cancellations, Greenpeace also noted that  “hundreds of thousands of euros of public funds were wasted just on the preparation of the project documentation required for the EIA. As much as we welcome the fact that the project will not be implemented, the fact that any investment was made in its preparation at all has drained money from real decarbonization measures."  [19]   [20] .

headline: Residents of Washington Park and South Providence successfully organized to defeat a proposal to build a waste transfer station in their neighborhood.
description: Residents of Washington Park and South Providence successfully organized to defeat a proposal to build a waste transfer station in their neighborhood. The facility would have processed 2500 tons of waste daily and created particulate pollution and environmental odors which would have negatively impacted the quality of life and health of those who live, work, and play in the area.  The 1.8 miles of Allens Avenue that runs along the Port of Providence is “arguably the most unpleasant stretch of road in Rhode Island,” according to journalist Frank Carini. [1] Marked by noxious odors from industry, diesel fumes from cars and trucks, and giant piles of materials such as scrap metal, asphalt, and road salt, many of the businesses on Allens Avenue have created negative health impacts for people in the nearby neighborhoods of South Providence and Washington Park, which have some of the highest asthma rates in the state and country. The lot at 481 Allens Avenue has hosted many polluting industries since the 1950s, including metal casting, scrap-metal processing, and waste storage. As a result, the site is classified as a brownfield because the soil has been contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbons, lead, and arsenic. [2] Operations on the site were written up several times over the years by the RI Department of Environmental Management (DEM) for safety violations, improperly stored material, and taking unauthorized items. The site sits next to Motiva, a petrochemical distributor; National Grid, a natural gas liquefaction facility; and Univar, a chemical processing plant, and is across the street from Meeting Street School, a school inclusive of students with disabilities that serves early childhood through grade eight students.  On Feb. 18, 2018, William Thibeault of Allens Providence Recycling LLC, a company based out of Everett, Massachusetts, bought 481 Allens Avenue for $950,000. [2] Between 2018 and 2020, the lot was used as a scrap-metal recycling facility and a tow yard. In December 2019, Allens Providence Recycling announced plans to build a construction and demolition (C&D) waste transfer station at the site. Residents were outraged at the proposal, as the project would further burden neighborhoods already bearing the brunt of a myriad of environmental harms. [3] The proposed facility would handle 2500 tons of residential waste, commercial waste, and construction debris daily, all of which would be brought in and removed by truck. This would result in an estimated 188 truck deliveries daily. These trucks would have to idle in a queue outside of the facility or circle the area if the queue was full, increasing the diesel pollution on Allens Avenue and nearby areas. [2] Residents also voiced concerns about the lack of adequate dust and odor control plans. C&D facilities produce fine particulates, which are especially dangerous because they can be inhaled into our lungs and/or be absorbed into our bloodstreams. Fine particulates are linked to cardiovascular diseases and short-term breathing problems, including asthma. Odors reported by residents, likely associated with volatile organic compounds (VOCs), lessen quality of life and cause health symptoms, including headaches, nausea, and respiratory irritation. The facility had no odor control plan, and its only dust control plan was to spray the facility with leachate, the liquid that accumulates from trash dumped onto the waste processing floor ( sometimes called “garbage juice”). Leachate has been found t o contain toxic heavy metals and PFAS (also known as “forever chemicals”). [4] PFAS can increase cancer risk, cause problems with fertility and pregnancy, compromise immune systems, and interfere with natural hormones and with liver, thyroid, and pancreatic function. [5]   A group of activists led by Linda Perri of the Washington Park Association and Monica Huertas of No LNG in PVD (now the People’s Port Authority), along with support from their city councilor, Pedro Espinal, quickly got their community involved in opposing the project. A meeting was held on January 8, 2020, to strategize and prepare for an upcoming City Planning Commission (CPC) hearing that would address the project proposal on January 21. [3] Seventy-five ( 75) community members attended the CPC hearing to oppose the project, which took place at 4:45 in the afternoon. [6] As journalist Steve Ahlquist noted, “Going to a public hearing that begins at 4:45 pm in downtown Providence is a very difficult thing for many people. It requires leaving work early and finding parking downtown during rush hour. It requires missing classes or losing paying wage hours at your job. It means securing childcare, transportation, [and] paying for parking.” Despite the efforts many residents went through to attend the meeting, they were told once they arrived that the company and requested a last-minute continuance, such that the agenda item had been postpone d. Residents who had shown up and wanted to speak were not allowed to do so, even though the CPC could have voted to allow them to do so under RI’s Open Meetings Act. Undeterred, they moved outdoors, into the cold winter evening, and held an impromptu rally with speeches against the transfer station, where activists vowed to come back with an even stronger turnout for the next meeting. [7] In the interim, the Racial and Environmental Justice Committee held a visioning session for residents to describe what they wanted the Port to look like going forward, and the Washington Park Association organized another community meeting with several elected officials and organizers to gather more opposition to the transfer station. [13] In late February, Providence City Council members, including Pedro Espinal, introduced a resolution calling on the CPC to deny the proposal. [8] This resolution amplified the concerns of community members and those raised in a staff report about zoning. 481 Allens Avenue is zoned as General Industrial (M-2), which allows for “a facility for the incineration and/or processing of waste, including sewage disposal facilities or solid waste transfer station, operated by or for a state or municipal agency.” [9] However, because the proposed transfer station would not be operated by the state or the municipality, it would not be allowed under current zoning laws. In the lead-up to the rescheduled CPC meeting on March 17, No LNG in PVD ran a door-knocking campaign to encourage neighbors to turn out for the meeting. Contextualizing th e transfer station within the longer fight for environmental justice in the Port of Providence, Monica Huertas of No LNG in PVD told volunteers, “It didn’t start with the transfer station and it’s not going to end with the transfer station. It’s not going to end on March 17, and even if the City Council says no, or whatever, this is not where it ends with the Port and all the issues we’re having with the Port.” [10] Ahead of the March 17 meeting, Allens Providence Recycling asked for another extension on their application, and then withdrew the application shortly afterwards. [11] While community members argued that the transfer station never should have been proposed at all, they celebrated the victory that the transfer station would not be built. Linda Perri of the Washington Park neighborhood association declared, “This was a win for the community. It is so great that everybody got behind this. It became a movement. It showed that real people really do care about injustice and the climate. It put a laser-like focus on South Providence. I would like to see that land developed into a green, clean solar field, something to benefit the community.” [12]

headline: National Grid built a natural gas liquefaction at Fields Point in Port of Providence despite vast opposition from residents in the nearby South Providence and Washington Park neighborhoods.
description: National Grid built a natural gas liquefaction at Fields Point in Port of Providence despite vast opposition from residents in the nearby South Providence and Washington Park neighborhoods who were concerned that the facility would create additional dependency on fossil fuels in the state and increase air pollution in their communities which were already burned by asthma rates. Natural gas is responsible for nearly 90% of energy generation in Rhode Island. [1]   The vast majority of this natural gas is produced in Appalachia, the Gulf Coast, or Canada and is transported to Rhode Island by pipelines developed and operated by Algonquin Gas Transmission Company and the Tennessee Gas Pipeline (TGP) Company. [2] On its coldest days  (around nine days per year), when an additional supply of natural gas is needed, Rhode Island relies on Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG), which is transported into the state via tanker truck. [3] LNG is produced as a liquid in facilities by cooling room temperature natural gas by around 162 degrees Celsius. The LNG is then transported and reheated to a gas form once it reaches its final destination, in a process known as regasification. Regasification is costly and extremely energy-intensive. National Grid, a British multinational electricity and gas utility, began operating an LNG storage facility at Fields Point in the Port of Providence in 1974, and in 2015, the company proposed building a liquefaction facility to produce LNG at the site. [4] When justifying the need for this facility, National Grid cited demand for more LNG from their customers, Narragansett Electric Company and Boston Gas Company, both of which are their own subsidiaries. [3] The Fields Point site is located near the residential areas of South Providence and Washington Park, which resident Gina Rodriguez described as “a beautiful, diverse, vibrant, strong Black and brown community.” [5] In the neighborhoods surrounding the proposed facility, 75% of residents are people of color, 56% are low­ income , and 17% are linguistically isolated. [6] South Providence and Washington Park are directly adjacent to the Port of Providence, where air, water, and soil pollution are produced by toxic industries, including fossil fuel infrastructure, petrochemical facilities, asphalt plants, and scrap yards. The air pollution from the port contributes to the neighborhoods having some of the highest childhood and adult asthma rates in the state. As soon as the liquefaction facility was proposed, community groups quickly mobilized to oppose it. The “No LNG in PVD” coalition was formed to spearhead the charge. Monica Huertas, an environmental justice advocate and mother of four from Washington Park, served as the coalition's coordinator. The Coalition which was made up of environmental justice groups, including the Environmental Justice League of RI (EJLRI) and FANG (Fighting Against Natural Gas), and youth-led activist groups, such as the Providence Youth Student Movement (PrYSM) and the Providence Student Union (PSU), began attending public meetings and hearings, holding street protests, and producing research to demonstrate the harms this facility would cause. [7] Residents communicated how the liquefaction facility’s existence posed a direct and immediate threat to their health and safety, and was fundamentally misaligned with their vision of a cleaner, safer, climate-resilient port for the following reasons: The facility would pose significant risks of natural gas leaks and explosions, which have notably occurred at other LNG facilities, including a liquefaction plant in Skikda, Algeria. [8] The facility sits close to the Rhode Island Hospital Complex, which contains the only Level 1 trauma center in the state, Women and Infants’ Hospital, and Hasbro Children’s Hospital, all of which could be impacted by an accident at the facility. [9]  The increase in truck traffic from tankers transporting LNG from Fields Point to other storage facilities will worsen air pollution and asthma in the neighborhoods surrounding the facility.   In the event of hurricanes or storm surges, LNG spills could be caused by flooding or storm surges. The facility would sit unprotected on the coastline and would have no emergency access once the water rises. The project would lead to an increased dependence on natural gas in Rhode Island, which is fundamentally misaligned with the residents’ interests and the city and state’s stated goals of transitioning to renewable energy. [10] Some of these fears were brought to bear when there was a major gas leak at the Fields Point LNG storage facility on March 29, 2017. 19 million cubic feet of natural gas and about 2 gallons of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) were released. [11] The leak led to the shutdown of the I-95 highway as response crews took measures to prevent a deadly explosion. Residents could hear and see the leak from their homes. Residents argued that if the current facility was already being mismanaged in ways that posed serious safety threats to their community, they could not trust National Grid to ensure safety at the new liquefaction facility. [6] From the outset, the processes for accessing information about the project and participating in the public approval process were made difficult for community members. Dates and times of public meetings were not available on National Grid’s website; rather, residents had to individually email the company to gain access to that information. All materials about the project published by National Grid were written solely in English, making the information unavailable to the large Spanish and Khmer-speaking populations in the neighborhoods impacted by the project. [12] And when residents did make it to public meetings, they were heavily policed, reinforcing a lack of recognition of challenges between local police and residents. Indeed, one meeting was even held in the Providence Public Safety Complex, which made many residents of color, who represented the majority of people impacted by the project, feel unsafe. [5]   Additionally, the required Public Participation Plan that National Grid submitted to the Federal Environmental and Regulatory Commission (FERC) included numerous nearby fossil fuel and chemical facilities like Univar, Sprague, Energy, and Motiva. The only community organizations included, the South Providence Neighborhood Association and the Washington Park Neighborhood Association, were either not in existence or inactive at the time the plan was released. [13] At a public meeting that the community had fought for months to have, Gina Rodriguez directly called out National Grid representatives for the lack of transparency in the process, declaring, “The fact that you keep calling this a public engagement process or a public involvement plan when we’ve had no involvement and no input is a farce. It is a lie. And it just shows how racist you are.” [5]  After the fraught initial public meetings held by National Grid, the next phase of the process began: the Coastal Resources Management Council’s (CRMC) approval process. CRMC is a planning and regulatory agency that oversees activity in Rhode Island’s coastal zone. The council includes staff scientists who serve in advisory roles and politically appointed voting members. In summer of 2017, a few months before the CRMC was set to hear the National Grid case, Rhode Island Governor Gina Raimondo replaced three environmentalist members of the CRMC whose terms had expired (there is no limit to the number of terms members can serve; most had only served 1-2 terms despite the norm being at least two full terms). [14] They were replaced by Lisette Gomes, Michelle Collie, and Jennifer Cervenka, the latter of whom was appointed as the new chair of the council. [15] The makeup of this council was much more favorable to National Grid, whose employees contributed $20,165 to Governor Raimondo’s campaign between 2014 and 2017. [17]   A public CRMC hearing on the project was scheduled for November 14, 2017. So many community members showed up to testify that an additional hearing was scheduled for November 28th. [18] At the second hearing, more than 50 people testified for over four hours. Residents implored the CRMC to consider how these facilities would impact their children, who were already growing up in a neighborhood surrounded by environmental hazards. Members of the council showed disinterest in residents’ testimony, including by looking at their phones, demonstrating particular disrespect towards testifying residents of color, such as when Chair Jennifer Cervenka interrupted activist Justice Gaines’s testimony about environmental racism. [18] Cervenka and CRMC member Grover Fugate walked out during resident Gina Rodriguez’s testimony and called on police to surround her. [19]   In response, No LNG in PVD issued a letter condemning Cervenka’s actions and calling attention to potential conflicts of interest that she had failed to disclose before presiding over the National Grid Case. Cervenka was previously employed at a law firm where Robin Main, who represented National Grid in the CRMC hearings, was a law partner and had oversight over her. [20] Cervenka also served as the chair of the RI Chamber of Commerce Coalition, an organization whose members have various professional ties to National Grid. Cervenka held this position concurrently with her position on the CRMC. [21] After No LNG in PVD’s letter was published, 427 community members, 32 organizations, and 9 elected officials called for Cervenka’s resignation from CRMC. [22] Cervenka ignored these calls, and days later, the CRMC unanimously issued its approval of the facility after nineteen minutes of deliberation. [23] In the following months, the project also obtained the necessary permits from the RI Department of Environmental Management and was approved by the Federal Energy and Regulatory Commission (FERC). [16] After multiple construction delays, the project was completed and became operational in May 2023. [24] [25]   In 2020, No LNG in PVD became the People’s Port Authority, shifting its focus to combat systemic problems in the regulatory oversight and decision-making processes in the Port, in addition to continuing to fight against harmful projects like this one. [26]

headline: Amid soaring gas prices and Russia-related tensions, Italy placed a Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU) in Piombino to boost LNG imports. The project sparked protests over environmental risks, limited local benefits, and fossil-fuel dependence, mobilising unions, citizens, and environmental groups, reflecting decades of industrial decline and social frustration.
description: Normal 0 false false false EN-GB X-NONE AR-SA /* Style Definitions */ table.MsoNormalTable {mso-style-name:"Table Normal"; mso-tstyle-rowband-size:0; mso-tstyle-colband-size:0; mso-style-noshow:yes; mso-style-priority:99; mso-style-parent:""; mso-padding-alt:0cm 5.4pt 0cm 5.4pt; mso-para-margin-top:0cm; mso-para-margin-right:0cm; mso-para-margin-bottom:8.0pt; mso-para-margin-left:0cm; line-height:115%; mso-pagination:widow-orphan; font-size:12.0pt; font-family:"Aptos",sans-serif; mso-ascii-font-family:Aptos; mso-ascii-theme-font:minor-latin; mso-hansi-font-family:Aptos; mso-hansi-theme-font:minor-latin; mso-font-kerning:1.0pt; mso-ligatures:standardcontextual; mso-fareast-language:EN-US;} In the context of heightened natural gas prices and geopolitical tensions with the Russian Federation that characterised 2022 and 2023, the Italian government chose the port of Piombino as the docking place for a new FSRU (Floating Storage and Regasification Unit). An FSRU is a maritime vessel designed to receive, store, and convert liquefied natural gas (LNG) back into its gaseous state for distribution into the onshore gas grid. According to its proponents, importing LNG and injecting it into the national gas grid via FSRUs moored in Italian ports would increase supply and reduce reliance on pipeline-delivered gas from Russia. However, critics argued that the project threatened local ecosystems, offered limited economic benefits, and reinforced dependence on fossil fuels. This led to widespread protests, including street demonstrations, public assemblies, appeals to administrative courts, and campaigns organised by trade unions, local associations, and environmental groups, highlighting the population’s frustration with both the FSRU and decades of industrial decline. The first confirmation that Piombino had been chosen to host an FSRU came on 6 April 2022, when Roberto Cingolani, then the Minister for Ecological Transition, announced to the Chamber of Deputies' Foreign Affairs Committee that the port would accommodate a regasification plant for a period of one or two years. [1]  According to SNAM, the part state-owned company to which the government had already entrusted the management of new FSRUs, Piombino was chosen because of its central location on the Italian peninsula, its proximity to the National Gas Transportation Network, and the suitability of its existing port quay for docking an FSRU. [2] Piombino is a medium-sized coastal city in southern Tuscany whose economy has long depended on large state-owned steelworks that shaped both employment and urban life. From the 1980s onwards, privatisation and successive industrial crises triggered a gradual deindustrialisation. Following privatisation in the 1990s, decades of industrial decline, failed investments, and recurring promises of regeneration left the area marked by unemployment, pollution, and social fatigue. Repeated unfulfilled plans for redevelopment fostered a deep mistrust toward institutions and a shared sense of economic stagnation. [3] [4] The government's plan was met with immediate suspicion by local authorities and businesses, due to the lack of consultation and the evident fact that the FSRU would occupy a large part of the port. [3]  In this sense, the government’s attempt to deal with this matter as quickly as possible was the initial cause of friction between the Ministry and local communities. In an effort to reduce opposition, the Minister organised several meetings with local and regional authorities, [5]  promising that as a compensation Piombino would soon benefit from plans to revitalise its industrial sector, [6]  and later appointing Eugenio Giani, the President of Tuscany, as Special Commissioner for the FSRU project. [7] Despite government assurances, opposition to the project intensified as details emerged. Local administrations and associations raised environmental and economic objections: the daily discharge of around 50 kilograms of chlorine into the sea threatened marine ecosystems;  the construction of an 8-km pipeline risked disrupting the landscape and port activities;  and local fishermen feared damage to fish and mussel farms. [8]  Additionally, Greenpeace and WWF warned that the terminal’s location in a marine sanctuary endangered protected cetacean habitats. [9]  The government’s decision to bypass standard environmental assessments, citing urgency, further eroded public trust. [10] At the same time, the Federation of Basic Unions (USB) condemned the project for diverting space and investment from sustainable redevelopment of the historical steel and tourism sectors, industries capable of creating far more employment than an FSRU requiring only about twenty specialised workers and creating no prospect of long-term local development. [11]  Similar concerns were cited by local businesspeople and industrialists, as well as by all local sections of national parties across the political divide. [1]  This unusually broad mobilisation reflected not merely environmental and economic concerns related to the FSRU, but a wider frustration rooted in chronic unemployment, industrial decline, pollution, and decades of political disillusionment. [3] Beyond the local level, national and international environmental groups challenged the project on systemic grounds. Legambiente, Greenpeace, and WWF criticised it as part of a broader expansion of fossil-fuel infrastructure that prolongs dependence on methane, a major greenhouse gas subject to significant leakage throughout its supply chain. They argued that this policy perpetuates extractivist and neo-imperialist dynamics, linking Italy’s energy security to environmentally and politically destabilising practices in the Global South. [9] [12] Despite the early concerns and widespread opposition, in June 2022 SNAM acquired Italis LNG , a 293-metre vessel capable of storing 170,000 cubic metres of liquefied natural gas and regasifying up to five billion cubic metres annually. [2]  Preparatory works in the port continued throughout 2022, and on 19 March 2023 the vessel was moored at the eastern quay of the northern dock. [13] During this preparatory phase, opposition in Piombino unfolded on multiple fronts. At the grassroots level, public assemblies and street demonstrations were organised by citizens’ committees, local branches of all major parties, trade unions (with USB even calling for a general strike [14] ), and national environmental organisations.  [3] [13] [15] [16] [17] [18] [19] [20] [21] [22]   The mobilisation extended beyond the local context: activists from Ravenna joined in, connecting the two movements opposing FSRU projects launched under the same national LNG expansion plan. [22] [23] [24]  At the institutional level, municipal authorities submitted dozens of critical observations to the authorising committee [25]  and filed appeals before administrative courts. [26]  In response to the mobilisation, the government’s only concession was to formalise the FSRU’s three-year operation. [8]  Meanwhile, no progress was made on the promised compensations outlined by the President of Tuscany, which included long-delayed projects such as road access, environmental remediation, and plans for the FSRU’s eventual relocation. [27] In all other respects, the government and regional authorities remained firm: the observations were disregarded, [28] and the administrative court dismissed all appeals. [29]  After technical adjustments and testing, operations officially began in July 2023. [13] Opposition to the FSRU in Piombino eased after its launch, becoming one of many grievances linked to local deindustrialisation. Tensions resurfaced in 2025 as the three-year operational period neared its end. SNAM’s CEO and the President of Liguria announced plans to move the Italis FSRU offshore near Savona, Liguria for 17 years. [30] [31]  Local organisations in Liguria opposed the move, echoing Piombino’s earlier concerns, prompting the regional council to vote against the transfer. [32] In March 2025, ARERA, the national energy regulator, argued that relocating the regasification plant installed two years earlier would be too costly and recommended it remain in Piombino, contrary to government agreements from 2023. [33] [34]  The local section of Confindustria, the main organisation representing business interests, also shifted position, endorsing the FSRU’s stay as potentially beneficial for port development. [35] So  far, opposition to the departure has been limited, mainly a signature-collection campaign, far less mobilised than the initial protests.

headline: Greenpeace activists occupied a gas terminal, calling attention to the environmental impacts of LNG and the need to phase out gas.
description: On April 29, 2023, Greenpeace activists blocked Fluxys ’ LNG terminal in Zeebrugge [1] . On rubber boats and kayaks, they entered the terminal and attached a “Gas kills, Fluxys guilty” banner to the terminal’s loading and unloading quays [2] . The occupation lasted 6 hours, after which the activists were removed by police, and 14 of them were detained for 48 hours.  Fluxys, a Belgian gas operator, operates a 12,000-kilometre pipeline network across Europe [3] . The company’s LNG terminal in Zeebrugge is an important re-exporting hub for Russian LNG. Since the beginning of the war in Ukraine, European imports of LNG from the United States increased by 140%  [2] . Greenpeace wants to raise attention to the role of gas operators like Fluxys in the stark increase of US-based LNG to Europe. Gas projects have severe environmental and climate impacts  [1] . The organization demands a halt to new gas infrastructure projects and a European-wide plan to phase out gas by 2035. Two years later,  eight activists from Greenpeace Belgium confronted an LNG tanker coming from the US, and heading for the port of Zeebrugge. "They approached the US Marvel Swallow   and unfurled banners featuring Trump and Putin, and reading “Their gas, your cash” to denounce how Europe’s reliance on fossil gas fuels geopolitical instability, while leaving households burdened with skyrocketing energy costs".  On board the Arctic Sunrise,  Joeri Thijs, spokesperson for Greenpeace Belgium , said: “Autocrats like Putin fund their wars with gas revenues, while political bullies like Trump use their dominance as gas suppliers to pressure European countries economically and politically." headline: Environmental impacts, labor issues, and opposition to the regasification plant.
description: Introduction The liquefied natural gas (LNG) regasification plant is located in the Port of Sagunto, Valencia, with a storage capacity of 600,000 m 3 . Since 2021, and especially since 2022 with the Ukraine war and sanctions on Russia, activity at the regasification plant has increased significantly due to rising imports of U.S. fracked gas. [1] This growth has led to labor conflicts, environmental risks, and protests from environmental organizations like Greenpeace and other local social movements. The plant was inaugurated in 2006 amidst real estate speculation and construction booms preceding the 2008 financial crisis, spurred by the bipartisanship of Spain’s PP and PSOE parties, despite significant local opposition [2] . Although it faced controversy from the beginning and international environmental commitments had been made (such as the 1997 Kyoto Protocol in effect since 2005), the plant was approved and inaugurated on June 26, 2006, next to a town of 44,000 people, a marshland designated as a Special Protection Area for endangered birds, and surrounded by the infrastructure of the Port of Sagunto [3] .  Case History In 2006, in Spain, during the speculative real estate and construction bubble that affected the entire country leading up to the 2008 crisis, the state, under the PSOE administration, initially financed the construction and expansion of the regasification terminal at the Port of Sagunto (Valencia) with €390 million from the European Investment Bank, eventually investing over €500 million in the project [4] . Notably, by then, the 1997 Kyoto Protocol had entered into force just a year before construction began, in 2005, alongside other conventions and agreements such as the UNFCCC, signed at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992, which paved the way for the later Paris Agreement in 2015. In this context, the construction of the Port of Sagunto regasification plant was approved on 23 hectares reclaimed from the sea. The main private investors include the operating company Saggas, whose shareholders are Enagas, Osaka Gas, and Oman Oil Company [5] holding 72.5%, 20%, and 7.5% of the shares, respectively [6] . Notably, both Enagas and Osaka Gas have major shareholders, including the U.S. fund BlackRock and Spanish billionaire Amancio Ortega [7] . However, the plant’s construction cannot be fully understood without considering the public relations strategies [8] —such as those promoted by the International Gas Union to encourage public acceptance—that Unión Fenosa (the original promoter of Saggas’ Sagunto plant) implemented. Their efforts included economic development contributions (direct and indirect), support for local industry, campaigns promoting pride and belonging in Sagunto, and essential energy infrastructure for Spain [9] . Social Mobilization and Protest The political party Esquerra Unida requested a study in the Valencian Parliament on the risks and potential accidents [10] at the regasification plant, given its proximity to Fertiberia’s fertilizer plant, which could trigger a domino effect in the event of an accident or fire. These concerns add to the allegations from the local environmental group Acció Ecologista-Agró Camp de Morvedre, who filed complaints in 2021 with the Valencian Government about Saggas' ship-to-ship LNG transfer activities at the regasification plant. The group highlighted the dangers of normalizing these operations for the environment, workers, and Sagunto’s residents.  In 2021, Greenpeace protested against fossil fuel use by blocking [11] gas unloading from a tanker at the regasification plant, leading to the arrest of the *Esperanza*’s captain by the Guardia Civil on a Sagunto judge’s order. Though released the next day, he faced charges for allegedly disobeying authorities. Police and judicial investigations were also launched against Greenpeace. The organization’s actions are part of the larger fight against climate change and the push to end fossil fuel reliance, such as LNG and fracking-derived natural gas.  Consequently, the gas terminal, along with other industrial activities at the port, has become part of a “sacrifice zone” where socio-environmental impacts are concentrated. In February 2002, Unión Fenosa’s Environmental Impact Study on the Sagunto Regasification Plant (published in the Spanish Official Gazette by the Ministry of the Environment [12] ) identified 85 negative environmental impacts versus only 28 positive ones [13] . Among them, it highlighted risks such as “Population disruption due to major accidents” and “Air quality disruption due to major accidents,” along with numerous impacts on marine vegetation and fauna, expected to last throughout the plant’s 50-year operational life. Despite these concerns, the regasification plant was installed and continues its activities as of 2024. Labor Conflict Starting in 2022 and the ramifications of the Ukraine war, there has been a surge in LNG imports derived from U.S. fracking, resulting in a substantial increase in activity at the regasification terminal. This has led the workers of Amarradores del Puerto de Sagunto CEMSA-P&REYSER to file complaints with the local council, accusing the company of violating legal working hour limits, which have increased from 1,820 to 2,500 hours annually. Additionally, they reported breaches in labor and HR standards, claiming that the company has not adequately adapted its resources to safely handle the increase in mooring and unmooring services following the rise in LNG import activities. These violations have led to work-related accidents, temporary disabilities due to stress and overwork, and have compromised worker health and safety [14] .  El Marjal del Moro A unique feature of the Saggas regasification plant’s location, as well as the Port of Sagunto, is their proximity to a marsh that provides habitat for endangered bird species: El Marjal del Moro. This ecologically valuable area was designated a Special Protection Area for Birds (SPA) in 1995 under the European Birds Directive (2009/147/EC) and is part of Spain’s Natura 2000 network. Article 8 of the directive stipulates that “the preservation, maintenance, or restoration of a diversity and sufficient area of habitats is essential for the conservation of all bird species.” [15] . According to *Métode.cat* (2013), the marsh's plight is “the result of silence from environmental organizations and the media.” [16] . The publication points out that the marsh’s proximity to chemicals, gases, noise, and truck traffic “does not seem to be a good combination of factors for its survival.” It also warns that Saggas’ massive use of seawater could impact marine currents and sedimentation and erosion areas, which over time could transform the marsh into a beach, increasing the risk of urban development speculation. EU-Funded Greenwashing In a greenwashing , twist, Saggas has committed to offsetting 20 tons of CO2 equivalent [17] , annually from its Sagunto regasification plant. For context, the average individual in Spain emits between 5 and 9 tons annually [18] . However, a 2023 report on Saggas’ emissions reveals that total emissions exceeded 170,000 tons of CO2 equivalent (direct and indirect) for that year [19] . Furthermore, a study by Robert W. Howarth (2024) [20] , found that a complete 38-day LNG shipment cycle generates 7,370 g of CO2 equivalent per kilogram of transported LNG. Given that a storage tank can hold approximately 67,500 tons of LNG, a single shipment generates an estimated 460,000 tons of CO2 equivalent during the 38-day trip.  This mitigation project estimates a reduction of “1,517.79 tons of CO2 equivalent over the project’s 10-year duration.” [21] . This is a clear example of greenwashing , supported by European institutions and public funds under the LIFE Wetlands 4 Climate project, coordinated by the Global Nature Foundation, which is part of the European Commission. Current Project Status  Since the Ukraine war began in 2022, the Sagunto regasification plant has seen a sharp increase in activity. Sanctions against Russia and the sabotage of the Nord Stream pipeline have led to a marked rise in LNG imports to Spain, primarily sourced from U.S. fracking. This practice has shown devastating effects on public health and the environment in the U.S., especially in marginalized communities. The toxins from fracking are linked to serious health issues, including leukemia, liver damage, eye and respiratory irritation, and migraines (Fractracker, 2023) [22] . Scientific studies have concluded that no fracking method is risk-free for human health or climate stability (Physicians for Social Responsibility, 2023) [23] . These activities disproportionately affect Black, Latino, and Indigenous communities, exacerbating social and health inequalities (Gonzalez et al., 2023) [23] . Furthermore, fracking threatens aquifers and has led to soil contamination in drought-affected areas like Texas (New York Times, 2023) [24] .  According to Greenpeace, these imports increased by 1422% [25] between 2017 and 2022. The increase in activity, along with that of the Port and other industrial entities in the area, has had adverse effects on El Marjal del Moro, which is not in good conservation status and has seen its ecosystem altered, as observed in the *Radiography of Spain's Wetlands* report (Global Nature Foundation, 2023) which highlights that only 13% [26] of Spanish wetlands are in good condition.

headline: Cove Point LNG export terminal, located in Lusby, Maryland, raises concerns among residents of the Calvert County. Its environmental impacts have created conflict due to its contribution to air and noise pollution, global warming, and biodiversity loss. Local environmental groups are pushing for a shift towards renewable energy to replace the LNG project.
description: The Cove Point liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal in Calvert County, Maryland, is at the centre of a conflict between local residents, fishermen and Dominion Energy, the company that operates the facility. Originally designed to import LNG, the terminal has been converted into an export facility, in line with the growth in US gas exports to international markets [1] . J. M. Neal, along with local residents and fishermen, is leading the opposition to Dominion Energy's conversion of the Cove Point LNG terminal to an export facility, citing environmental risks such as air and water pollution, including methane emissions, that threaten the Chesapeake Bay ecosystem [2] . Dominion Energy has begun transforming the Cove Point terminal into an LNG export platform as part of a nationwide trend in the US to tap into large reserves of shale gas for sale overseas. The company has emphasized the economic benefits of the project, such as job creation, increased local revenue, and a significant contribution to US energy exports [1] . The move is designed to take advantage of growing international demand for natural gas, particularly in Europe and Asia. Stakeholders involved in this case are: Dominion Energy: the main comapny operat ing the terminal, responsible for LNG exports  [2] . Local and federal authorities: they supported the project, considering it essential for energy security and the economy [2] . Local residents and fishermen: led by Jean Marie Neal and other activists, they oppose the project because of its environmental and social impacts [2] . Environmental Justice Organizations (EJOs): groups such as the Sierra Club have joined the opposition, highlighting the risks to the Chesapeake Bay ecosystem [2] : - The Sierra Club campaigns against the project, focusing on air quality and marine life preservation [4] . - Chesapeake Climate Action Network (CCAN) opposes the project advocating for climate action and protection of the Chesapeake Bay [2] . - Earthjustice provides legal support to halt the project, filing lawsuits on behalf of community groups [5] . - Cove Point Natural Heritage Trust works to protect local biodiversity and mitigate industrial impacts [2] . - Local Homeowners' Associations (Cove of Calvert) represent residents' concerns about safety, property values, and quality of life [2] . - Calvert Citizen for a Healthy Community advocates for health and environmental protection through community outreach and awareness campaigns [2] .  - National and Local Politicians (e.g., Senator Ben Cardin, and Congressman Steny Hoyer) raised concerns and called for stricter environmental assessments and oversight [2] . Opponents of the project are expressing concerns about public health, safety, and the environment. For example, local residents fear an increase in respiratory illnesses due to high levels of nitrogen oxide and particulate emissions for the terminal's operations [2] . Methane emissions are also a major concern, as this strong greenhouse gas could increase climate change and contribute to long-term health problems, including headaches and nausea for neighbouring communities. In addition, the risk of industrial accidents, such as explosions or toxic leaks is increased by the proximity of high-pressure pipelines and storage facilities [2] . Fishermen in the Chesapeake Bay region fear that the increased maritime traffic and industrial pollution resulting from LNG exports could significantly harm fish and crab populations, which are cr itical to the local economy  [2] . Residents also fear a deterioration in the local quality of life due to the noise and visual nuisance caused by the industrial infrastructure. The expansion of Cove Point is contributing to the increasing industrialization of the region, putting biodiversity of the Chesapeake Bay at risk [3] . The Bay is home to species of fish and shelfish essential to the local economy, and pollution could affect their habitats. Environmental Justice Organizations (EJOs) like the Sierra Club have raised concerns over the project's environmental impact, particularly the risks posed to marine life and public health, arguing that the expansion of LNG infrastructure contributes to industrialization and ecological degradation [4] . Although natural gas is presented as a cleaner alternative to coal, extracting, transporting, and liquefying it requires large amounts of energy, increasing the project's carbon footprint.  The Sierra Club and other environmental groups such as the CCAN have taken legal action by filing a lawsuit against Dominion Energy, accusing the company of failing to fully assess the potential environmental and health impacts, particularly the effects on the Chesapeake Bay's biodiversity and the community's air quality [5] . However, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) in charge of taking the decision finally approved the project [6] . The EJOs are campaigning for a switch to renewable energies, believing that the expansion of fossil fuel infrastructure is a step backwards in the fight against climate change.  One of the main points of controversy is the proximity of the terminal to residential areas. The residents of Cove Point live less than two kilometers from the facility and are exposed to risks related to pollution and industrial accidents. In addition, the deterioration in air quality, the increase in maritime traffic, and the activities linked to the terminal could affect people's health, particularly by increasing the risk of respiratory illnesses [7] ,  or poisoning due to water contamination [8] . The Cove Point project illustrates the growing tension between perceived economic benefits, as defined by Dominion Energy and local authorities, and environmental protection. Dominion Energy claims that the expansion of the facility is economically beneficial because of job creation, increased local revenues and its contribution to US energy exports. However, these benefits are essentially based on short-term gains that do not take into account external costs, such as environmental degradation and public health risks. As Kapp (1950) pointed out in The Social Costs of Private Enterprise, these economic evaluations often neglect the long-term social and environmental impacts, passing on these hidden costs to local communities and ecosystems [9] .

headline: The Repauno Chemical Company initially produced dynamite and other chemicals. The site expanded into producing various organic compounds and materials over the twentieth century. Environmental contamination from hazardous chemicals led to state-mandated cleanups and investigations starting in the 1980s. Now, the polluted site is in the process of being turned into an international shipping port.
description: The Repauno Chemical Company (Repauno) was founded in Gibbstown, New Jersey, on June 7, 1880 by Lammot du Pont, the grandson of the EI du Pont de Nemours Company (DuPont) founder. [1] Repauno produced a range of products including dynamite, acids, nitrobenzene and other organic compounds [2] . Lammot du Pont was killed in an 1884 explosion at the Repauno plant, and DuPont bought the Repauno plant and became the country's largest dynamite producer. In 1902, the Eastern Laboratory, DuPont's first research laboratory, was built at the Repauno site to conduct explosives research. [3] Prior to the onset of environmental regulations in the 1970s, companies did not keep track of and report spills. Records of spills and other releases were kept at the Repauno Site starting in 1976. Between June 4, 1976, and April 03, 2012, 506 records of incidents related to air, soil, water, and unclassified releases occurred at the Site. [3] According to the 2002 Annual Groundwater Progress report, the area previously used by DuPont as a terminal location for anhydrous ammonia is being cleaned for reuse. In addition, several different companies currently lease areas at the Repauno facility. [4]   In the 1980's, a zone on the site, referred to as the Lower Aquifer was discovered to be impacted by contamination of several organic constituents above NJ GWQC, including benzene, TCE, PCE, nitrobenzene, aniline, naphthalene, chlorobenzene, and 2,4-DNT. [4] In 1990, the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) required DuPont to conduct a Remedial Investigation and Feasibility Study of 12 solid waste management units and 11 areas of concern at the site. [4] 8,500 tons of sediments were removed from the ditches in the former Nitrobenzene and Pyromellitic Dianhydride/Dimethyl Terephthalate production areas. [2] DuPont sold the remaining business operations, with Repauno Products LLC purchasing the manufacturing operation that produced sodium nitrite and nitrosylsulfuric acid in 1998. In 1999, Spring AG purchased the industrial diamond refining operation, which was closed in 2002. Despite the business sales, DuPont retained ownership of the property. [1] As of August 2003, DuPont had completed four phases of the required RI. [4] Due to the contamination, the property was labeled as a brownfield site, a "real property, the expansion, redevelopment, or reuse of which may be complicated by the presence or potential presence of a hazardous substance, pollutant, or contaminant. " [6]   Discussions began of turning the land into a port. In 2009, the Gloucester County Improvement Authority (GCIA) and the township of Greenwich entered into an agreement to be equal partners in the redevelopment of 280 acres of the 1,700-acre property, to build a port. [7] However, the recession stalled the discussions of a port. [7] [8]   In January 2012, the EPA filed a lawsuit against a company that improperly demolished and removed asbestos-tainted materials. The EPA alleged six violations of the federal Clean Air Act and the National Emission Standard for Hazardous Air Pollutants (NESHAP) regarding asbestos. “Lovett failed to take required precautions in demolishing or removing about 5,000 feet of piping and 3,000 feet of pipe insulation with amounts of asbestos that could be exposed to the air…The EPA is asking the court to assess a $32,000 penalty per violation, per day , on the company. It's also asking for the costs of the suit.” [9]   While several businesses were making bids for the land in August 2012, the mayor, George Shivery was quoted saying “I feel like we need something clean, that won't have a possible affect[sic] on the land or health” , including that Greenwich township has “first right of refusal” on any project, and would use it if the plan would negatively affect the land. [10] On February 1, 2015 DuPont's spinoff company, Chemours FC, LLC became a new site's owner. In August of 2015, State Senate President Steve Sweeney held a press conference announcing the sale of the entire property to Fortress Investment Group. The price of the sale was not disclosed. [11] The investment group “aimed to turn the dormant 1,800-acre property into a port-related industrial park for imports and exports.” [12]   On June 30, 2016, Chemours sold approximately 125 acres located along the Delaware River in the north-central portion of the property to Fortress Investment Group, who passed the property off to a subsidiary company, the Delaware River Partners LLC, who renamed the site the Repauno Port and Rail Terminal in the summer of 2016. [13] “Chemours retained all responsibility for the necessary remediation and other activities related to the contamination present on the property sold to Delaware River Partners, LLC.” [3] The plans still encompassed creating an industrial park “including a number of cold storage warehouses, underground storage tanks for butane, and an eventual port for importing and exporting goods.” Another planner stated that the plan would include “a working port for cold storage of fresh and frozen fruits and flowers. The site would also work as a new vehicle receiving depot and a location of fuel activities.” Initially, the plan had included the storage of liquid natural gas, but after the Sierra Club Chapter of New Jersey (SCCNJ) mobilized support against it, the plan was altered to store butane instead. The director of SCCNJ said in response to the proposal for the property "they must come out against this proposal because Delaware River Partners plans to transport hazardous materials through communities and ship them right on the Delaware River. This facility will have greater safety implications for people living near the River, while threatening our public health and the environment".  [14] Additional mobilization occurred with the creation of the Concerned Citizens for the Redevelopment of the Repauno Site (CCRRS), who called for the property to continue to be remediated, but not developed into a highly trafficked area. [14]   In 2017, a proposal was submitted by DRP for the state to approve a “Delaware River dredging and deep water berth construction project for the proposed DRP Gibbstown Logistics Center, a multi-use marine terminal and international logistics center. The project involves dredging 371,000 cubic yards (cy) of sediment from the Delaware River, to a depth of 40 feet below (-40) mean lower low water (MLLW) to construct the deep-water berth. The project also involves demolition of the existing wharf and bulkhead, along with the construction of a new bulkhead, a new pile-supported wharf structure, and six new storm water outfall structures.” [15]   A “duly noticed” public hearing was mentioned in the proposal. [15] On March 27th, 2019, The NJDEP Commissioner announced and filed 4 new, public lawsuits organized by the New Jersey Department Of Environmental Protection; The Commissioner Of The New Jersey Department Of Environmental Protection; And The Administrator Of The New Jersey Spill Compensation Fund against DuPont, Chemours, and 3M. Part of the lawsuit focuses on contamination of groundwater, surface water, and other natural resources caused by releases of volatile and semi-volatile organic compounds, mercury, lead and other contaminants from the DuPont Repauno site. [16] [3] [17] In April 2019, Former President Donald Trump issued an executive order expediting the approval of energy infrastructure, including but not limited to oil and gas pipelines. [18] An additional order was issued that removed much of the steps required of companies obtaining permits for infrastructure projects involving US international borders, such as bridges, tunnels, pipelines, or land transportation routes. [19]   [20] Despite immense protest from environmentalists at a public hearing, [21] the Delaware River Basin Commission unanimously approved the proposal to dredge a portion of the river and build a $96 million 1,600-foot-long pier to load tankers in June 2019. The DRP proposed to export large volumes of liquid fuels produced from fracking Pennsylvania shale gas wells, and it was approved. [22] One journalist, Meg McGuire, wrote of the hearing: “The usual routine for the DRBC is to gather (and study) between 15 and 30 "dockets' (its word for projects) and present them together at a public hearing where speakers can address the commissioners about any of the projects on the list (or submit written comments for a period of time.). Last Thursday, June 6, 2019, the DRBC called an unusual public hearing for a single project…And with a limited written public comment period that ended about 24 hours after the hearing.” [23]     Upon contacting both the DRBC, McGuire was directed to contact the NJDEP. It was then that the NJDEP disclosed in a “commitment to transparency and public engagement, including in its permit review process” that on May 20, 2019, the NJDEP had issued a Waterfront Development Individual Permit to Delaware River Partners. On June 5, 2019, the DEP had suspended the permit due to a procedural error. Corrective notice was published in the DEP Bulletin on June 5, 2019, with a 15-day public comment period from that date, at which point the DEP would reconsider the permit. [23] Activists rallied against this proposal, and formed a coalition, EMPOWER NJ. [24] In December 2019, the Trump administration approved the shipment of liquefied natural gas from fracking fields in Pennsylvania to the Repauno Site.  [25] The Trump era LNG by rail rule allows for trains with up to 100 tank cars, each with upwards of 30,000 gallons of LNG, to move through the country's cities and towns. [26] The New Jersey State, along with 14 other states, filed a challenge to the federal rule with the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit on August, 18th, 2020. [27] Simultaneously, six environmental advocacy groups, represented by the nonprofit environmental law organization filed a separate challenge to overturn the rule. In response, the DRP filed a petition to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission  for a declaratory order, a loophole that would make LNG operations at the site not subject to the approval of the federal agency in September of 2020. [28] [29]   The Delaware Riverkeeper Network filed a challenge to the petition. [30]   In December 2020, despite the massive mobilization efforts by environmentalist groups and the community, the 2017 petition to dredge part of the Delaware River and to construct a new wharf designated specifically for LNG export was approved in a 4-0 vote. [31] [32] In November 2021, PHMSA, with the Federal Railroad Administration, proposed reversing the 2020 rule by the Trump administration that broadly allowed LNG by rail. “PHMSA said it had received 7,000 comments about reversing the Trump-era rule.” [33] In May 2022, the NJDEP proposed new rules to regulate underground storage caverns for holding “any natural or artificial gas, or any petroleum product or derivative of any petroleum product.” [34] In August 2022, an in-depth article was published regarding the May NJDEP proposal and environmental justice and overburdened communities impacted by underground storage in New Jersey [35]   In 2023, The US Department of Transportation denied the 2020 special permit request by Energy Transport Solutions (subsidiary of New Fortress Energy) which would have allowed the transportation of liquefied natural gas by rail to the Repauno port. [36] [37] [38] .

headline: Ruwais LNG planned Terminal will export LNG to other countries and other regions of the country. The Terminal’s construction, however, has raised concerns over potential health and safety risks faced by low-skilled migrants’ workers.
description: Liquified Natural Gas (LNG) is seeing an expansion in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The country is currently exporting 5 mtpa (million tonnes per annum) [11] , and according to Bloomberg, it is expecting to almost double their LNG capacity by 2027, and four-fold it by the end of the decade. [1] The expansion of LNG is driven by increased global gas demand from other countries, and from Europe in particular, as Europe is attempting to find alternatives to Russian gas. [2]  According to OEC 2022 data, the top 5 destinations of LNG from UAE are India (47%), Japan (28%), South Korea (9%), Taiwan (6%), and Thailand (4%). [3]  As of 2022, exports to European countries only accounted for 2%, including France, Spain, Belgium and the UK, [3]  however, according to Climate Home News, several other European countries such as Germany or Austria are currently turning to the UAE to cover their needs. [2] The UAE currently has 3 LNG Terminals, Das Island (export), Ruwais (import) and Jebel Ali (import), which are distributed along the coast and in Das island, see Figure 1. [4]   Besides these, another LNG Export Terminal is planned in Ruwais expected to start operations in 2028. [5] The construction of LNG Terminals and distribution networks, however, has raised concerns over occupational health and safety risks faced by low-skilled migrants’ workers. Several cases have been raised by workers of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), [2]  who owns both Ruwais Terminals (located in Al Ruwais Industrial Park, west of Abu Dhabi) and the one at Das Island. For the purposes of this case study, Ruwais LNG export Terminals is at focus, but occupational health and safety risks could be present at any of ADNOC’s owned facilities.  Al Ruwais Industrial Park is home to many of ADNOC’s operations. Because of this, ADNOC decided to move its LNG planned export Terminal from Fujairah to Ruwais. [5]  The Terminal, with an expected  two liquefaction trains and 9.6 mtpa (million tonnes per annum) capacity , has been designed to be powered by renewable energy and nuclear power, being the first facility in the Middle East and North Africa to run on “clean” power. [5]  In 2024, BP, Mitsui & Co, Shell and TotalEnergies took 10% stake each of the Terminal, with ADNOC retaining 60% stake. [6]  Public statements from the international companies who joined Ruwais project highlight how the low-carbon aspect of the Terminal is aligned with their decarbonisation values or strategy, [6]  despite the Terminal being used to export liquified natural gas, which is not renewable. Buyers of LNG from Ruwais include China (Zhijang province), [7]  Germany, who signed a 15-year Heads of Agreement with Energie Baden-Württemberg for the delivery of 0.6 million mtpa [8] and another one with SEFE (Securing Energy for Europe), [9]  and India, with Indian Oil Corp announcing to buy one million metric tons each year from the terminal. [10] Concerns over health and safety risks of workers of ADNOC has been raised in multiple occasions and according to Climate Home News the construction of Terminals in UAE and Qatar will rely of low-skilled migrant workers. [2]  Instances of labour abuse in the UAE oil and gas sector and in ADNOC’s operations in particular have been raised by workers (anonymously) and international NGOs. [2]  Workers and industry observers state that the oil and gas sector has improved safety protocols, but there is no transparency and conflict of interests in work-related injuries, accidents or deaths. [2]  According to Fair/Square, an international NGO, not all deaths and incidents are being investigated, particularly when the accidents involve non-nationals and low-skilled jobs. [2]  An engineer of ADNOC states that accidents are rarely reported, there is no transparency or accountability. [2]  According to a low-skilled ADNOC worker, despite being aware of the dangers of his work he prefers working in the oil and gas sector as it is better paid than in other sectors. [2]  Wages, however, do not seem proportionate to the high risks low-skilled workers undertake, according to an ADNOC engineer. [2]   Moreover, ADNOC hires third party contractors for construction and engineering, who rarely hold the same standards as ADNOC. [2]
