headline: Named after the mythological Celtic Otherworld, the Mag Mell is a Floating Regasification and Storage Unit of liquid natural gas, proposed just 50km from the coast of County Cork. The facility is one of three that was proposed in the country, and met with resistance from campaigners who are fighting to keep Ireland free from fracked gas, and thus LNG-free.
description: The US company Predator Oil & Gas planned the development of ‘Mag Mell’ Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU) for Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) located in the Muir Cheilteach (Celtic Sea) 50km off the coast of County Cork. [1] Its capacity was planned to be 3.3 bcm per year, and would be composed of two floating storage units, that would use the disused Kinsale Head gas pipeline to transport gas to shore. [1] Utilising the Kinsale Pipeline was cited by the Mag Mell project organisers as a benefit of the project, allowing a “key piece of physical infrastructure” [10] to stay in use, emphasising their desire to repurpose old existing oil and gas infrastructure [11] . Following much resistance from campaigners in Ireland (with support from international anti-gas groups), the government put a ban on importing fracked gas, which led all proposed LNG projects in the country to be halted or paused. Yet, this ban was overturned by the government in 2023, who cited the necessity of “national energy security” in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the energy precarity that followed. The struggle to keep Ireland LNG free - and, thus free of fracked gas - continues.  Project and resistance timeline In 2020, Predator set up an Irish subsidiary (Predator LNG Ireland), and employed the Irish environmental consultant, SLR Environmental Consulting, as regulatory, planning and environmental advisors to help advance their project, amidst uncertainty around whether their project would be halted by the government. [2] At the same time, two other LNG facilities were further along in their planning process, with strong opposition from the public and civil society organisations such as Not Here Not Anywhere, Safety Before LNG, Love Leitrim and Friends of the Earth Ireland  [3 ]  [4] [12] , with initial support from Irish Green party politicians. These facilities were Hess Corp’s “Shannon LNG” terminal and NextDecade’s “Cork LNG” terminal. In June 2020, Eamon Ryan, the Green Party Minister for Energy in parliament tweeted Safety Before LNG stating “ be rest assured, if we can agree to the #PFG [Programme for Government] we will implement the policies which will see an end to the importation of fracked gas via any LNG terminals in Ireland”. As a result of these organisations' tireless campaigning, including several court victories [10] , in 2021, all of these LNG projects were successfully halted or paused, following the government's ban of all fracked gas imports. In the policy statement on the importation of fracked gas that was published on the 18th of May 2021, Eamon Ryan states, “Fracked gas causes environmental damage both locally where it is extracted and globally and Ireland, having banned its exploitation onshore, should not impose these environmental risks on other communities around the globe”. [5] Although the explicit statement from the government stated that they were ruling out all “commercial LNG Terminals” for the foreseeable, it was deduced that this meant all LNG terminals, seeing as LNG relies heavily on fracked gas from the US - a 2023 report from Food & Water Action Europe and Gastivists found that “fracked US gas could represent as much as one eighth of all gas the EU consumed in 2022”, adding that 87% of the gas extracted in the US is fracked [6] .  Yet, Predator’s FSRU project was only shelved, and in November 2023 when the “Energy Security in Ireland to 2030” report was released, it demonstrated the government's U-Turn on the banning of fracked gas through their support of “state-led” LNG’s to ensure energy security for the country. State led simply means commissioned by the state, and “does not preclude a public-private-partnership nor the involvement of private firms contracted to provide, build or operate the necessary infrastructure”, according to the 2023 report. [7] Following this, in March 2024, 150 groups wrote an open letter [9]   to the Green Party Minister for Energy, calling for a confirmation that he and the Green party would stand by their word, and not use the excuse of ‘national energy security’ as a reason to allow for an LNG terminal to be established in the country. Most of these groups were Irish, however there was notable international support from Concerned Health Professionals of Pennsylvania and North American fracked communities that are already negatively impacted by the fracking of gas in their regions. [8] In the lead up to local and EU elections of June 2024, Not Here Not Anywhere complied the report "Keep Ireland LNG Free" in response to the "Energy Security in Ireland to 2030" report [13] . Their report demaned that councillors must make a pledge against the Mag Mell project if they are claiming to take climate change, inlcuding the Irish Climate Action Plan of 2023 (CAP23), as well as the interests of the Irish people seriously. The report highlighted issues with this proposed FSRU, which include security concerns, pollution impacts and issues with leasing, specifically mentioning that as this units intended purpose is only "in the event of a supply shock" ,  the project is merely "an expensive insurance policy" measure [13] . On June 16th, 2024, the US-based organisation Frack Action organised an information event "Don't Blow Up Cork" about the risks of the FSRU. [15]   The event was held in Cork city, and included a panel presentation with spe akers including Julia Walsh (Director at Frack Action, Eoghan Harris (Founder at Future Generations Kerry), Amber Morningstar (Byars Choctaw activist) and moderation by Roisin Myers (Cork resident and youth climate activist).   [16] On June 19th, 2024 Not Here Not Anywhere came together with Frack Action and Friends of the Earth (FoE) to brief the politicians in Leinster House, Ireland on the dangers and risks associated with the FSRU, highlighting the work of Not Hear Not Anywhere's recent report [13] .  The event was hosted by Neasa Hourigan TD, a member of parliament for the Greens. During the briefing, Julia Walsh again discussed the 2024 Biden administration's ban on new export terminal permits. While Jerry Mac Evilly (head of policy at FoE) briefed parliament members on the importance of resisting a U-turn position on LNG by standing by the strict climate measured that the government itself have proposed. Mide Power spoke on behalf of Not Here Not Anywhere to share information from the organisations   "Keep Ireland LNG Free: Unpacking the Energy Security Review & Detailing How a Floating Storage and Regasification Unit Will Impact Ireland's Climate Goals" report.  [14]    The push by international oil and gas companies to add Ireland to their global LNG network has been tirelessly opposed by trans-atlantic activists for nearly a decade. This conflict displays an inspiring example of how civil society can hold politicians to their word, demonstrating a kind of democracy that today can seem absent in a western context.

headline: An LNG import terminal project on the East German island of Rügen has been approved by the German Ministry of Economic Affairs. The local community is strongly opposed to the project, which they consider harmful to the environment and the economy.
description: Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the world's economic powers are trying to find alternative sources of energy supply. This has prompted Germany to take an interest in the subject, and especially liquified natural gas (LNG). The LNG Acceleration Act of 12 July 2023 provides the basis for eleven (eight floating and three on shore) new LNG terminals in various locations such as in Mukran on the island of Rügen  [1] . The gas would arrive at Rügen by ship from all over the world and be converted and stored in a Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU). The project includes the creation of pipelines to transport the gas. The platform, located off the coast of Rügen, is connected to the gas network "with a 38-kilometre offshore pipeline through the ecologically highly sensitive Bay of Greifswald" [6] . The project was unveiled on 13 February 2023 by the Ministry of Economic Affairs [2]  and approved by the government on 7 July 2023. Deutsche ReGas began construction during the summer and the terminal is due to come on stream by the first semester of 2024 [1] . However, the project has led to a number of demonstrations and protests, as many stakeholders do not agree with it. The main criticism is that with a projected capacity of 13.5 billion cubic meters per year (bcm/y) the project regasification capacity is totally oversized for the needs of the country. The project also risks potencial damage to the environment. Rügen is a tourist island in Germany, and locals fear that tourism will decline because of the increased air pollution and the impact this will have on the island in the long term. The island will lose some of its beauty. Ecologists also fear the impact of this infrastructure on coastal and marine ecosystems. This project does not promote the use of renewable energies at all, but rather the gas industry. And it goes against existing climate legislation of the country [3] .   The main environmental impacts can be simply divided into two categories: air pollution and soil contamination. T here are methane leaks during the production, transport and processing of LNG; methane is a greenhouse gas 80 times more harmful than CO2. It leaks into the atmosphere throughout the production and supply chain and slips directly from the ship’s funnels, contributing to climate warming at a significant pace [11] [12] . As a result, producing LNG will speed up global warming and Germany will not reach its climate targets because of additional emissions of methane. As  the LNG production chain involves the use and the combustion of a huge amount of fuel which produces a lot of CO2 emissions. Indeed, air pollution is the most serious impact of LNG expansion  [4] . LNG terminals also release air pollutants that threaten the health of local residents, including tons of sulfur dioxide (which damages the lungs), nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds (both of which contribute to smog), microscopic soot or particulate matter (which can trigger asthma and heart attacks), and carbon monoxide (which can inhibit oxygen intake to the heart and brain)  [13] . LNG terminals are also reported to cause chemicals,  such as volatile organic compounds, nitrogen oxides, and benzene, seeping into the soil and groundwater. This poses social and health problems to the local population [14] . And it also presents an immediate threat to disrupt local fishing grounds [13] . There are also economic issues at stake in this project. The growing demand for gas in Europe is driving up global gas prices, with consequences in the countries of the Global South such as power shortages and power cuts [5] . In response, various protests have been taking place against the construction of the project. On 8th May 2023, Fridays for Future Germany, alongside Bürgerinitiative Lebenswertes Rügen (Rügen Worth Living citizen's initiative), Deutsche Umwelthilfe (DUH, Environmental Action Germany ), and other organisations protested in front of the Federal Chancellery while a petition to cancel the project signed by 61000 people was being discussed at the Bundestag [16] . Sascha Müller-Kraenne from DUH expressed that "The federal government is going against common sense in climate policy and against the people on the island. Rügen, like Lützerath, will thus become another symbol for the federal government's inadequate climate policy." [17] A poll confirmed that the opposition to the project is generalised, only 35.6% of Germans supports building an LNG terminal there, with 49.6% against and 14.8% undecided, a survey by Civey showed in March  [15] . On July 7th, Binz municipality announced a legal challenge against the construction of the project at the Federal Administrative Court [18] . The DUH also filed a lawsuit against the project at the Federal Administrative Court challenging the fast-tracked approval process of the project that did not meet basic environmental requirements [19] . The lawsuit specifically refers to the approval of a 38-kilometer-long connecting line from the mainland coastal town of Lubmin to Rügen, which poses a great threat to marine ecosystems.  [16] On 7 September 2023, Greenpeace activists also protested against Rügen LNG [1] . Greenpeace claims that w ith oversized LNG projects like in Rügen, Germany is cementing its dependence on fossil fuels for decades to come.  However, in order to meet the climate targets, gas consumption and thus also the volume of LNG imports must fall drastically in the coming years. This project therefore raises many questions and a great deal of discontent. The question is whether it will be completed and under what conditions and at what cost for the environment and for people. In a noteworthy demonstration opposing the use of fossil fuels, members of Greenpeace, the environmental protection organization, temporarily interrupted the construction of the pipeline conneting the future LNG terminal to the gas network in the Greifswalder Bodden, Germany. This unexpected protest featured four to five inflatable boats surrounding the pipe-laying vessel "Castoro 10." Furthermore, two individuals ascended a portion of the pipeline, unfurling a banner with the impactful statement "Gas destroys!". Ende Gelände, a civil disobedience movement occupying coal mines in Germany to raise awareness for climate justice, staged against Rügen LNG on 22-24 September in 2023. They proposed to prevent the construction of the Rügen LNG terminal before the gas infrastructure is built. The group used itscharacteristic tactics to occupy the construction site of the pipeline en masse [20] Otherwise,  ENDE GELÄNDE host two climate camps to well prepare the protest  against the expansion of fossil energies and for climate justice on 23 September  [5] . On the political front, Manuela Schwesig (SPD), Premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania (the state in which Rügen is located), has “publicly opposed the federal government's plans to authorize the LNG terminal on the island” [9] . In addition, Karsten Schneider and Kai Gardeja, mayor and tourism director of the seaside town of Binz on the island of Rügen, are trying to have the project cancelled so that biodiversity and tourism are not impacted by the negative effects of such a project [9] .

headline: Le Havre LNG Floating Storage and Regasification Unit aims at breaking away from Russian gas imports and obtain other sources of gas supply for France. Several environmentalists are opposed to this project as they believe it undermines the local environment and that it is not useful.
description: Le Havre Liquefied natural gas (LNG) Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FRSU) is located in the Bougainville Sud Dock in the port of the city Le Havre in Normandy. It was prompted by the war between Ukraine and Russia. The EU, including France, had been importing gas from Russia in large quantities before the war. The main purpose of this project is to break away from Russian gas imports and obtain other sources of gas supply for France [1] [2] [3] .   The FRSU vessel is named Cape Ann and is managed by TotalEnergies through its subsidiary TotalEnergies LNG Services France (TELSF). GRTgaz (a subsidiary of Engie) is in charge of the 3.5 km pipeline running under the city canal that links the FRSU to the French gas network. Haropa Port, manages the port of Le Havre and is in charge of the reception of the FRSU. The FRSU arrived in the port of Le Havre on September 18, 2023, but was not yet in use at the beginning of October 2023. As for now, the plan is to use it for 5 years at a capacity of 5 bcm /y [1] [2] [4] [5] [6] .     The project was actually adopted by the public authorities on Friday, July 29, 2022   [7] . From the decision to conduct no environmental assessment for the construction of the pipeline, several administrative authorizations were granted for onshore installations as well as derogations  [8] . Le Havre FRSU is a controversial project as many environmentalists are opposed to it due to its environmental impacts  [4] .  It contributes to greenhouse gas emissions and therefore to global warming, as it requires the use of fossil fuels, notably shale gas for LNG [9] . The carbon footprint of this project is significant, as it requires considerable energy to cool it at the start and to heat it on arrival. This leads to air pollution [10] . Le Havre FRSU may also lead to a loss of biodiversity, particularly in marine spaces [11] . The four land-based LNG terminals located in France (Loon-Plage, Montoir-de-Bretagne, and two in Fos-sur-Mer) are subject to the Seveso-III Directive on the control of major-accident hazards involving dangerous substances. Because the Le Havre gas terminal is a floating installation, it escapes the Seveso directive. However it is at the heart of an area comprising 21 Seveso factories and t he proximity to these sites multiplies the dangers to the environment  [9] [12] . Proponents of Le Havre FRSU have claimed that the project has potential economic impacts benefits such as job creation. However, it can also affect energy prices on a local level as LNG is known to be expensive  [13] .   Le Havre FRSU has potential social impacts particularly related to health and safety of local populations. The project is located less than 2 km from the "Les Neiges" housing quarter in the city of Le Havre, which due to its proximity, may be exposed to various safety issues such as accidents involving leaks or explosions, or noise pollution  [11] [14] . In addition, the proximity of this project to Seveso sites (containing materials that are hazardous to humans) multiplies the risks that could affect the health and safety of local populations  [9] [12] [15] . There may be a lack of safety in the workplace, with negative consequences coming from industrial activity on workers’ health [16] .     The firms TELSF, GRTgaz and Haropa were chosen to deal with one aspect of the project and they are driven by economic interests since by exploiting le Havre FRSU, they are making money. Haropa port which manages the port of the city Le Havre is in charge of the reception of the FRSU and by charging its own fees for the use of its infrastructures, it makes money [17] . GRTgaz is in charge of the pipeline that connects the FRSU to the French gas network and by exploiting it, it generates revenues [18] . TELFSF, the subsidiary of TotalEnergies is the main company in this project as it is responsible for the management of the FRSU and therefore by exploiting it, it can generate revenues. With this project, TotalEnergies can increase its LNG gas production capacity and resell it to other European countries while making profits in the process due to the strong demand for LNG in Europe  [18] [19] . The involved French public environmental authorities  (Ministry of Ecological Transition, the Seine Maritime préfecture, the Regional Directorate for Environment, Planning and Housing, and the intercommunal body Le Havre Seine)  [2] [18]   claim that this project is needed to meet energy needs and energy independence as well as to avoid the risk of a energy shortage  [17] [20] [21] .   The groups opposing to the project are mostly environmentalists, who are concerned about the damage to the environment associated with Le Havre FRSU. It includes the NGO Greenpeace, members of the group Scientifiques en Rebellion, representatives of the French environmentalist political party "Europe Ecologie-Les Verts" now called "Les Ecologistes", the Normandy branch of this same party, environmental assocations such as the association "Ecologie pour le Havre", Collectif Climat Le Havre, the French federation of nature and environmental protection associations called "France Nature Environnement" and the "Extinction Rebellion" movement. To better understand their role and position of each of these environmentalists, a chronology of different events is provided. Following a meeting on October 14, 2022 by the Normandy prefecture which aimed at presenting Le Havre FRSU to the public, Le Havre climate collective created a petition to obtain 1,000 signatures in order to create a public debate  [9] [15] .  On November 30, 2022, Julien Bayou, a deputy from the political party "les Ecologistes" of Paris announced his decision to file an appeal with the Council of State, aiming to stop the decree allowing this project. He has his own position regarding Le Havre FRSU: he said that no real danger weighs on the gas supply with the high level of gas stocks in Europe and that this should not validate its creation. He also added this project has negative impacts on the environment. He was supported by the Normandy branch of the political party and local environmental associations during that day  [20] . The “Ecologistes” party filed two other appeals aimed at stopping two building permits linked to the FRSU in Le Havre which were rejected on January 19, 2023  [21] . On Wednesday April 19, 2023, the France Nature Environnement federation said that it filed an appeal with the administrative court of Rouen (Seine-Maritime) against the FRSU project in Le Havre. It shares its position by saying that this project goes against the recommendations of the scientific community as well as French environmental objectives. Furthermore, the federation does not share the government's vision saying that a danger weighs on the gas supply and that there is no proof while France is doing well in terms of its gas stocks  [22] . In a press release on Wednesday, June 28, 2023 coupled with an investigation in partnership with Disclose (an NGO of investigative journalism), Greenpeace shares its position regarding the usefulness of the FRSU project in Le Havre. The investigation carried out by Disclose focuses more on the usefulness of the project and assumes that the creation of this FRSU is not necessary due to the fact that France already has enough stocks to meet its gas needs. The press release from Greenpeace contains two major points. LNG represents a fossil energy and contributes to GHG emissions even than more conventional gas. The NGO wants to move away from gas and fossil fuels and shifts towards renewable energies    [18] [19] [23] . On August 22, 2023, a fourth appeal was filed by Julien Bayou, the Normandy branch of Les Écologistes party as well as by the association Ecologie pour le Havre against an order taken by the prefect which authorized GHG emissions. Julien Bayou once again shared his opinion on the negative impact of this project on the environment as well as its uselessness  [24] . On September 16, 2023, members of the Extinction Rebellion movement and the association Ecologie pour le Havre joined in protest against the arrival of the FRSU in Le Havre. They carried out different actions such as giving leaflets  [10] . On September 18, 2023, members of Greenpeace blocked the route of the FRSU Cap Anne in the port of Le Havre with kayaks. They painted “gas kills” on the FRSU. Members of the group Scientifiques en Rebellion attended this event too claiming that the project is “an ecological, social and economic aberration”     [1] [10] . The last event dates from September 22, 2023 when members of Collectif Climat Le Havre demonstrated in front of the University of Le Havre at the time when a scientific festival conference was taking place. They intervened to point out the presence of TotalEnergies at this conference. They distributed leaflets to students and showed a banner revealing the FRSU threats  [25] .

headline: Plans for a LNG terminal to be built in the Port of Cork City by US Firm NextDecade have been shelved following much resistance from local, national and international civil society organisations.
description: NextDecade Cork FSRU is a Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) terminal proposed to be built in Ringaskiddy located in the western side of Cork’s industrial port. The project is owned by the US company NextDecade, and is designed to be an import terminal receiving gas from the USA. The project costs €125 million (151 million USD) in total, and would have the capacity of 4.0 billion cubic metres per year, that is 2.9 million metric tonnes of natural gas being transported through and stored annually. [1] It was in 2017 when the Port of Cork signed a memorandum of understanding with NextDecade and Flex LNG to install a Floating Storage Regasification Unit (FSRU) and associated LNG import terminal infrastructure in the port [1] , which marked the beginning of the consultation process [2] . The port is an ‘Irish semi-state’ [3] , meaning it is owned by the government, and is already a hub of industry and a major port for the country and, more widely, Europe. The terminal would be located right next to a Bord Gáis plant which is the state-owned gas company in Ireland, therefore it is in the Bord Gáis’ interest that the project goes ahead. Although it was never explicitly stated by the company that the purpose would be to import fracked gas, NextDecade already uses fracked gas in some of its explorations [2] and from the outset it was decided that gas from the Rio Grande LNG export terminal in South Texas was destined for the proposed LNG terminal in Cork. The gas would then be turned into fossil gas and pumped onto the main gas line from the Kinsale gas fields which run onshore in the Whitegate area [3] .  Resisting the project from its beginnings was the grassroots Irish environmental network Not Here Not Anywhere that is campaigning to end fossil fuel exploration and the development of new fossil fuel projects. It is a volunteer-run organisation at the forefront of campaigning for introducing an amendment to the Planning and Development Act to stop all LNG applications being granted in the country. [4] Other than their legislative campaigns, they also organised demonstrations, created a petition against the Cork LNG terminal [6] and communicated educational content on their social media platforms around the drawbacks and dangers of LNG [3]   that are often glossed over by fossil gas companies.  In 2018, they wrote an open letter to the Port of Cork signed by over 50 civil society organisations, including local organisations (Cork Climate Action, UCC Environmental Society, Cork Environmental Forum), national organisations (An Taisce Climate Committee, Irish Doctors for the Environment, Frack Free Clare), international organisation (350.org, Oil Change International, Friends of the Earth) and allied environmental organisation from around the world ( New Brunswick Anti-Shale Gas Alliance - resisting export terminals in eastern Canada, Citizens Movement Climate and health - a German group fighting the LNG terminal in Brunsbuettel, Save Rio Grande Valley and the Carrizo/Comecrudo Tribe - fighting NextDecade's Rio Grande LNG in Texas, US). The letter decried the hypocrisy of the Irish government if it were to accept the project: "In 2017 the Republic of Ireland banned fracking on health and environmental grounds. It would be morally corrupt to allow this project to proceed as it would facilitate the importation of fracked gas from the United States which has devastating impacts on communities, local environments and the climate." [5] .  Following this letter, in 2019, the Green party in Ireland brought forward the motion that encouraged councillors in the area to write to the Port of Cork and the Minister for Communications, Climate Change and the Environment (Richard Bruton) to immediately halt any plans that could involve the “the importation of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) extracted using hydraulic fracturing” [7] . All but one councillor voted in favour of the motion. The Green councillor for north central Cork, Oliver Moran, stated that “locating a storage terminal in Cork would be a test of the government’s credibility in meeting the challenges of the global climate and biodiversity crisis”. [7] Also in 2019, fellow activists from the southern Texas community group Save Rio Grande Valley joined local groups to hand in a petition against the project to the port authority. Rebekah Hinojosa from Save Rio Grande Valley said they “don’t want their communities to be sacrificed” so that “dirty fracked gas” can be exported to Ireland. Local activist believed that forging alliances with groups directly affected by the production of fracked gas would be could be an important way to stop the project [10] . For NextDecade’s LNG to progress to the next stages of development, it was dependent on a few things - European markets demand for shale gas being one of them. In November 2020, Engie, the French energy company, halted talks over a long-term supply agreement with NextDecade. This was due to pressures not to import shale gas [8] .  In January 2021, the Environment Minister Eamon Ryan announced it would not renew the licence to develop the project acknowledging the incompatibility of the project with the climate commitments of the country [9] . The project has therefore been shelved. This decision came following the resistance of the local environmental groups, supported by local communities and the work of the Green party politicians in parliament. This case marks the rise in popular sovereignty against fossil gas in Ireland and, more widely, Europe.

headline: The Shannon LNG terminal aims to facilitate the import of gas to Ireland, the UK and the rest of Europe. Opponents argue that building new fossil fuel infrastructure is not in line with COP21 commitments and directly pushes Europe into a carbon lock-in.
description: Shannon Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) terminal would be the first of its kind to be built in Ireland. It would be  located in the rural area of Kilcolgan, which lies between the two north Kerry villages of Tarbert and Ballylong ford on the southern shores of the Shannon [1] . The purpose of building this terminal is to facilitate gas imports from non-EU countries (such as the US) to Ireland, the UK and the rest of Europe. The terminal’s proposed capacity is said to offer up to 180,000 m3 of LNG storage capacity and regasification capacity of up to 22.6 million m3/d [16] . In 2003, the terminal was first proposed by Paddy Power, an Irish oil executive [2] . The company Shannon LNG was then established in 2006 - as a subsidiary of “Hess LNG”, a 50/50 joint venture between Hess Corporation and Poten & Partners [2] which are US multinational corporations.  Traditionally, the importation of gas has been bound physically by the location of pipelines - often coming from places such as Russia, Central Asia or North Africa. LNGs have opened up possibilities for gas transportation, making it easier than ever to store and transport fuel with less reliance on pipelines, diversifying supplier opportunities to places such as the US, Western Africa and the Middle East. Patrick Bresnihan, a geography lecturer at Maynooth University, refers to the way in which LNG developments such as Shannon LNG illustrate how “energy provision is always embedded in wider networks, which connect geographies, finance, state and private interests” [3] . This project was never solely about national or regional development - from its beginnings it was embedded in wider networks. Seeking to develop European energy supply and security.  In 2008, the An Bord Pleanala (Ireland’s national planning board) granted the company planning permission for a new interconnector pipeline [2] to be built between Ireland and the UK. This was an essential part of the project - the current interconnector pipeline is owned by Ervia (formerly Bord Gais), a state-owned utility, meaning that the costs of maintaining it would continue to be borne by Irish customers [3] . Both Ervia and the Commission for Energy Regulation of Ireland (CER) celebrated this decision, stating it was a victory for the Irish people, as it meant that the cost of pipe  maintenance would now fall onto Shannon LNG. The Shannon LNG Terminal would result in the old  interconnector gas pipeline with the UK becoming redundant. As a result, CER ruled that Shannon LNG would have to contribute to the costs of the two new necessary interconnecting pipes which transport gas between Ireland and the UK. Shannon LNG claimed the tariffs would cost them tens of millions and serve to subsidise their competition in the UK. Shannon LNG failed in a High Court action against the CER tariff scheme in December 2013 [4] .  Legal disputes such as these resulted in huge financial difficulties for Hess, and eventually led them to sell Shannon LNG in 2016 [5] . They had spent more than €67m trying to progress the project [5] . It is now under management by the US multinational New Fortress. The sale includes the rights to develop land owned by the Shannon Group (formerly Shannon Development) and planning permission for the terminal [6] .  Despite being financed by US multinationals, the project is also eligible for political and financial support (CEF-Energy funding) from the EU through its inclusion on the 2015 PCI (Projects of Common Interest) list [8] . The decision to include this project on the PCI list was contested by Friends of the Irish Environment [15] . The project was also cited by the European Commission as a future strategic hub for Europe's gas supply, which means it is eligible for low cost financing from the European Investment Bank (EIB) and accelerated planning and permit granting [8] .  Action from Environmental Groups: In 2008, Friends of the Irish Environment Ltd (FIE) and Raymond O’Mahony (a welder and representative from the Kilcolgan Residents Association) brought forward legal proceedings challenging the proposed development [9] . Kilcolgan Residents Association first formed in 2006, in efforts to mobilise community members against the project. It brings together people campaigning for environmental reasons, economic reasons (such as farming) and those concerned with the health safety of the local population - creating alliances within the community. With traction building, the association expanded into “Safety Before LNG”, a national campaign group [1] . FIE was first established in 1997 to create and maintain a network of conservationists and  environmentalists in Ireland. It works with these networks, often assisting them with legal cases for the environment in Ireland [10] . In the 2008 legal case both parties submitted their concerns in the court, arguing that the Health and Safety Association (HSA) had applied major accident regulations to the project, yet subsequently the technical advice on the development was inadequate [10] . These shortcomings were the foundation for their legal battle and successfully brought proceedings to a halt. Since then, Safety Before LNG has sought to bring a wide scope of issues concerning usage of the Shannon estuary to the public's attention. They set out arguments for why Shannon LNG should not go ahead. The first poses the option of “Farming or Fracking” [10] - stating that Shannon LNG emissions would equate to the methane emissions from 1 million cattle and would severely impact Ireland’s strict carbon budget, meaning that cattle farming practices will have to be altered. As many people living in rural Ireland’s work in agriculture and animal husbandry, this draws alliances between the environmentalists and the farmers of the area. The group is opposed to fracking due to the various associated environmental and societal impacts. These feelings are echoed by other environmental activist groups across Ireland, such as Love Leitrim - an anti fracking group based in the north of the country [14] . The second argument focuses on how the proposed LNG is not necessarily for the Irish people. They pose that the real issue of resource use in Ireland is because the country has become home to many international data centres - it is said that data centres in Ireland are now consuming more metered electricity than all of our rural homes put together [11] . Indeed, certain political decisions made by the government encourage international companies to establish headquarters in the country, as it remains strategically based within the European Union and in close proximity to the UK. Famously, part of the Irish government's enterprise policy includes large tax breaks for these companies and their employees [13] . Safety Before LNG argues that the government should really re-centre the debate around energy usage inequality before signing deals that put people and the environment at further risk. Addressing the needs of the Irish people instead of using their lands to house international companies.  The third points to controversial payments made from Shannon LNG to Kerry Council, that raises ethical questions. It is reported that a total of €4.1 million has been paid from Shannon LNG to the council in relation to the project [11] . Councillor Finucane of Kerry stated that these payments were simply “good faith contributions” [11] made by a company that was committed to the area. Safety Before LNG state that these payouts are a potential sign that agreements are being made on the basis of financial gain, with no regard for environmental or social impacts.  By June 2023, planning permission for the LNG Terminal had expired, meaning US firm New Fortress Energy is still seeking planning permission and the project remains in its assessment stage [7] almost 20 years following its conception. This case highlights the intricate web of connections that financial institutions, investors and global corporations have with national and European governments surrounding global energy provisioning [3] . It raises concerns about EU and investor commitment to a just transition, especially as there has been much local  concern surrounding this development. In September 2023, An Board Pleanàla finally rejected New Fortress' request, stating that "the development would be inappropriate pending review of Ireland’s  energy supply" [17] . The decision was based mainly on the governments stance on importation of fracked gas.

headline: Across the Yamal penninsula where already a mega Arctic LNG1 is in operation, a new LNG 2 project is under construction. Total (France) is very much involved.
description: Just across the Yamal peninsula, in the autonomous administrative region of Yamal-Nenets, where already a mega Arctic LNG1 is in operation [2] ; a new  LNG 2 project has been under construction [1] [2] . Namely, on the opposite side in the western part of the Gydan Peninsula [1] [3] .  Companies involved in this project are Novatek (Russia) (60%)- out of which Total (France) (10%), y Ekropromstroy (China) (40%) with an estimated investment of $25.5bn [1] . In 2018 it was announced in Paris on 24 May  in the presence of the President of the Russian Federation, Vladimir Putin, and the President of the French Republic, Emmanuel Macron, that Total signed an agreement with Novatek outlining the terms upon which Total shall acquire a direct working interest of 10% in Arctic LNG 2, a giant liquefied natural gas project lead by Novatek on the Gydan Peninsula in thevnorth of Siberia. Taking account of Total’s approximate 19% stake in Novatek and Novatek’s intention to retain 60% of the project, the Total Group's overall economic interest in this new LNG project will be approximately 21.5%. Should Novatek decide to reduce its participation below 60%, Total will have the possibility to increase its direct share up to 15%.  Novatek and Total have also agreed that Total will have the opportunity to acquire a 10 to 15% direct interest in Novatek'sfuture LNG projects in Yamal and Gydan.(13).  “Total is delighted to be part of this new world class LNG project alongside its partner Novatek, leveraging the positive experience acquired in the successful Yamal LNG project. This project fits into our strategic partnership with Novatek and also with our sustained commitment to contribute to developing the vast gas resources in Russia’s far north which will primarily be destined for the strongly growing Asian market." said Patrick Pouyanné, Chairman and CEO of Total. “Arctic LNG 2 will contribute to our strategy of growth in LNG by developing competitive projects based on giant low cost resources.”(13).  With a production capacity of approximately 19.8 million tons per year (Mt/year), or 535,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (boe/d), Arctic LNG 2 will unlock more than 7 billion boe of hydrocarbons’ resources in the onshore Utrenneye gas and condensate field. The project will involve the installation of three gravity-based structures in the Gulf of Ob on which will be installed the three liquefaction trains of 6.6 Mt/year capacity each. In the same way as for Yamal LNG, Arctic LNG 2 production will be delivered to international markets by a fleet of ice-class LNG carriers that will be able to use the Northern Sea Route for cargoes destined for Asia. (13). However, Gydan peninsula is home to Indigenous Nenets communities [2] [4] . They are already strongly affected by climate change. In winter 2020/2021 temperature variations connected to global warming led to the death of about 80,000 thousand reindeer in the Yamal Region [6] . Nenets are highly dependent on reindeer herding as a traditional way of life and feels increasingly powerless in the face of this "land grab". But this also leads to resistance, f.i. in the activities of an open group on social media [7] . The Arctic LNG 2 Project was also opposed by representatives of the reindeer herders themselves in an official complaint letters  to local municipality (early January 2021)  [2] . Further, the complain was also officially stated by community leaders in a newspaper [see 11]. Nenets strongly believe that a recent starvation of about 80,000 reindeers is directly related to gas projects and climate change of the whole peninsula [11] .  The degree of environmental protection of the area is decreasing: the federal Gydan reserve has lost its status and was converted into a national park in December 2019, which was interpreted by experts as making way for the development of the northernmost license area to secure long-term LNG production on the Gydan peninsula [10] .

headline: The Sabetta port is related to the Yamal gas mega project. Scientists and environmentalist warn about consequences of the accelerated Russian Arctic development.
description: Sabetta is one of the largest Russian Arctic ports situated on the Yamal peninsula, on the bank of the Ob River [2]. The port project was iniciated by the Russian Government as a project of strategic importance for the development of gas-rich Yamal Peninsula. The port is directely related to the Yamal Gas Mega Project. The extensive construction of transportation infrastructure is still ongoing in the scope of the Yamal project, including the Sabetta sea port [7] . Key companies of the port development include Novatek, the Federal Agency of Sea and River Transport, and the state enterprise Rosmorport [1] [4] .  The port covers an area of 60 ha. The project involves the construction of a 50km sea channel, a 6 kilometre long and 420m wide approach channel, and berths for construction materials cargo as well as gas tankers. The port also has a 4km  long canal for storage of ships, and a control station [1] . The port’s construction is being carried out in two phases. The piers for handling liquified natural gas plant modules and construction materials are being constructed in the phase one. Phase two includes the construction of berths for handling liquified natural gas and gas condensate [1] .  The dredging works performed at the port amounted to 1.5 million m³ of earthworks. A total of 25 million cubic meters of permafrost was excavated from the dredging of sea area and approach channel [1] . A cargo-vessel named "Yuri Arshenevsky", brought construction loads to the port with the help of nuclear powered ice-breaker called Taimyr [1] [6] . Activists from the Norwegian environmental group Bellona think that "Running a ship on LNG doesn't help the climate at all". Scientist working on the Arctic similarly stated "We are not sure how long the project will go on because of climate change"... "They build and sell  cheap gas and oil, but in the meantime, the Arctic continues to warm at twice the rate of the rest of the world." [2].  Also, the alternative environmental  media the Barents Observer and Eye on the Arctic -- web journalists from circumpolar countries-- constantly report on the project and rise concerns related to climate change, especially if the Arctic region will proceed with developments at the current speed or even more if it accelerates [4] [5] : "The whole route is now free of ice. "That is upsetting"... "This includes the East Siberian Sea, a region that normally has the longest-lasting ice cover" . ... "Air temperatures along the Siberian coast are generally 2 to 7 degrees Celsius above the 1981-2010 average" [8] ...Total of 94 vessels were sailing in the waters, many of them are transporting liquefied natural gas from the Yamal plant" ..."The ice had almost vanished in July 2019"  [8] . Navigation is helped by climate change that melts the ice, while the burning of fossil fuels increases climate change worldwide, and in particular in the Arctic. While activists, journalists, and scientist rise their concerns about the climate change, the government has a different perspective on the Arctic: the goal of the Sabetta port is an annual shipment of 80 million tons by 2024" [8] .  Scientist furthermore warn how developments on the Northern Sea Route are closely connected with current "dramatic" climate changes in the area: "2019 become the warmest year on record and ice melting is reaching unprecedented levels" [8] .

headline: Novatek obtained Arkticheskoye and Neytinskoye field for exploration which are a protected Arctic tundra and Indigenous lands. Chemical processing is part of the bigger project on the peninsula, including the Ob river case.
description: Novatek company from Russian Federation is operating the Yamal LNG and the company ambition is flourishing. These include the development of the Arctic LNG 2 and adjacent Gydan peninsula, and more recently, the Ob project based on the resources of the Verkhnetiuteyskoye and Zapadno-Seyakhinskoye fields [1] (see conflicts already documented in EJAtlas). However, a new natural gas project is underway [1,2]. Namely Arkticheskoye and Neytinskoye fields [1] . These newly obtained licence for exploitation are situated in  Yamalsky natural reserve, fragile Arctic tundra  [1] . Tundra refers to slow growing Arctic forest or no forest area of high biological and cultural values for Nenets Indigenous people, who use these lands for their livelihoods and local economise, such as reindeer herding [2] .  The Yamalsky reserve covers a 4,1 million hectare area, out of which  3,7 million are located in the central and southern part of the peninsula (see photos). According to Russian law, industrial activities are prohibited in nature reserves [1] . In fact, the Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Area is home to 13 specially protected areas of different categories [5] . Yet, this has not stop the company from exploiting the reserve and profit seeking. On the contrary, the borders of the Yamalsky reserve has  been adjusted following pressure from oil and gas companies, according to Barents Observer [1] .  For instance,  the first adjustment of the reserve was in 2013, at the same time as Gazprom moved ahead with the development of the Bovanenkovo project (see conflictive event in EJAtlas too). The latest border adjustment of the Yamalsky reserve was formalised in May 2021, only few weeks before Novatek had secured control over the licenses.  According to Interfax [3] , the field auction included special conditions that favoured Novatek and apparently no other company submitted interest in the fields. Moreover, this new conflict directly relates to the Ob LNG project. At present, Obsky LNG has been renamed into Obsky Mining and Chemical Combine - NOVATEK decided to produce ammonia and, possibly, methanol on its resource base. In addition to filling the resource base of Ob LNG, these fields "will make it possible to ensure the volume of production at Yamal LNG" ( it has already been built and is operating ), as well as to direct part of the LNG produced to the gasification of the Kamchatka Territory, "the head of NOVATEK noted [3] . This is why  the government of the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug to recommend changing the boundaries of the reserve [2,3].

headline: Russia’s biggest gas field covers two-thirds of the peninsula which the Nenets people need for nomadic reindeer-herding. For protesting, Nenets activists are accused of preventing economic development.
description: Nenets are an indigenous group that inhabits Yama peninsula, known as the Yamal-Nenets autonomous region in Russian Siberia [1] [4]. Being a nomad group, the Nenets migrate between forests or taiga to their grazing lands way up to Russia's northern fringe [6] . In the 1990s, however, as  90% of Russian gas can be found on the Yamal peninsula, Gazprom company under the Yamal LNG (Liquefied natural gas)   initiated preparations for one of its biggest gas projects, the Yamal Megaproject gas exploitation project promoted as renewable source of energy  [1] [6] .   Due to this mega project, Nentes' traditional lands have been transformed and environmental degradation started to take place [1].  “For them it is fortune, for us terror,” said 20-year-old herder. “The fact they’ve found deposits here is catastrophic”, another member of Nenets community stated [2] . Due to this project, some Nentes members left their traditional lands on the peninsula, as they refused a life in permanent settlements [1].  For those who stayed, the main problems are biophysical land degradation and the disappearance of cultural tradition. Their nomadic lifestyle and migration routes have been disrupted by gas infrastructure, pollution, and the effects of climate change [1].  But Nenets depend on reindeer-herding for their cultures and livelihoods. For example, warmer climate in the Arctic lead to a denser shrub growth across the tundra, making it more difficult for Nenets to gather and move reindeer herds. Extreme temperatures can cause freezing rain and ice that the reindeer herds can not graze or pass across easily [1]. In addition, the new pipelines and other industrial infrastructure are creating further obstacles to traditional migration routes [1]. Many activists from the Nenets community, especially the Forest Nenets, involved in Indigenous rights group alliances of Siberia, have publicly raised their concerns about the environmental challenges facing their community in order to raise awareness about the environmental and cultural issues of gas and oil industries on their traditional territories [1]. The activists have been holding seminars and training sessions, including legal issues, economic development, pollution and climate change [5]. In 2019, a Moscow court ordered the closing down of the Indigenous rights group, saying that the organization has not provided the correct documentation which is needed to be recognized by the Russian law [5]. But the group argued how the Russian Government accuses the community of trying to thwart Russian economic development [5].   The group’s allies say "this is a nonsense" and continue: "the alleged sentence is nothing but a pretext to silence the organization" [5]. “It’s not a legal issue. It’s a political one,”  Indigenous People of the North/Russian said. “There’s a big conflict of interest between corporations and indigenous people” [5]. The aim is “to frighten the society” [5].  "The organization also argued how the government built the gas plant ignoring climate change and crisis issues. The organization also argues how the development of such huge gas fields has other issues with permafrost holes, that can explode very easily, bringing a danger of large scale accidents to the community as well [5].  Gazprom, on the other hand, argues how they provide the Yamal province with $665 million a year, but did not comment on how exactly the money is distributed and to whom [2] . Herders and administration officials argue that compensations for pasture degradation and land are meant for local government but they do not reach Nenets people [2] . The community still argues how they do not want their cultural landscapes change: “I want my grandchildren to see our land as it is: beautiful, fresh, full of berries and deer” [2]

headline: By pushing for long-term exports of gas in a context where the Algerian public is excluded from decision-making and benefits are largely reserved for the regime’s elite, the EU is pursuing a gas grab.
description: Algeria is the sixth-largest gas exporter in the world, with more than 90% of its pipeline exports going to Spain (34%), Italy (27%), and other European countries. It is also the third-largest source of gas imports to the EU, accounting for 14% of gas imports and 10% of total consumption. Three pipelines currently link Algeria to Europe, and a fourth is being developed with Italy (1)   With reserves of 4.5 trillion cubic meters of gas, Algeria is the eleventh-largest natural gas reserves in the world and the second-largest reserves in Africa, behind Nigeria. The country is also estimated to hold the third largest amount of shale gas resources in the world (1).        An EU-Algeria Memorandum of Understanding for cooperation on oil and gas was signed in July 2013 between the European Commission’s President José Manuel Barroso and Algerian Prime Minister Abdelmalek Sellal. Barroso stated that “Energy is a priority area of the Euro-Mediterranean partnership... Algeria is a key partner for the EU. Natural gas is a strategic issue for both parties: Algeria is a major supplier to Europe, while Europe is by far the largest customer of Algeria.” (2)                         By pushing for long-term exports of gas in a context where the Algerian public is excluded from decision-making and benefits are largely reserved for the regime’s elite, the EU is pursuing a “gas grab.”          As Hamza Hamouchene (2016) puts it: “Words like “cooperation”, “integration”, as well as expressions such as “tapping Algeria’s huge unexploited reserves” and “diplomatic energy action plan” are all euphemisms for the EU’s aggressive attempts to grab more Algerian gas (be it conventional or non-conventional) while ignoring the Algerian people’s will and, in the case of shale gas, their grievances and preoccupations regarding their water and environment (2).                 At present there are several upcoming natural gas projects in Algeria involving a range of actors including partnerships between Algeria’s Sonatrach and GDF Suez, Repsol, RWE, Edison, Total, Cepsa, Partes, BG Group (now Shell), Statoil, Petroceltic and BP.

headline: The Company Sea-3 Providence aims to expand its storage and operations for liquid propane gas. Opposition suggests the proposal could continue the social and environmental harm from the industrial port. affecting a minority and low-income population.
description: The port of Providence, Rhode Island, (ProvPort) is a hub of industry, billed as “New England’s premier deep water multimodal facility for international trade and domestic distribution” [1] . The industrial port was sold by the city of Providence for $16.5 million and taken over by the private company ProvPort in 1994 [1] . There is a strong relationship between the private company and the city, as the port brings in large revenue for Providence. This includes a 19-million-gallon storage tank for liquid propane gas (LPG) owned by Sea-3 Providence LLC, which is looking to expand its operation through six 90,000-gallon horizontal storage bullet tanks. Along with the addition of new tanks, the 2021 proposal suggests a new pipe system to supply from the Providence River [4] [8] .  Environmental hazards in ProvPort include a scrap yard, propane tanks, a chemical plant, and water treatment facilities - all in an area with a low-income population and a high percentage of people of color. According to mapping done by the Environmental Protection Agency, the Washington Park and Lower South Providence neighborhoods located next to the ProvPort range from the 80th to the 95th low-income percentiles [6] . The demographic of this lower side of the city is 74%-97% people of color [6] [14] . Within and just outside these neighborhoods sit eight elementary, middle, and high schools, as well as the Johnson & Wales University campus. This area is also home to Providence’s healthcare hub just under two miles from the port and includes eight hospitals and nursing homes. The closest hospital, Rhode Island Hospital Center for Primary Care, is less than a mile from the Sea-3 site.  Current pollutants in zip code 02905, where Washington Park and Lower South Providence are located, include Xylene, Cyclohexane, Ammonia, and Benzene [2] . Xylene is obtained by distilling wood, coal tar, or petroleum, and is used in fuels. Benzene is a carcinogenic chemical, meaning it can cause blood cancers like leukemia and is harmful to the eyes, skin, airway, nervous system, and lungs [2] . As seen in national data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Rhode Island has the fourth-highest asthma rate in the country [5] . The national average of people suffering from respiratory conditions is 7.8% of the population, while in Rhode Island 12.1% of the state’s population has such conditions [5] [19] . Providence is ranked 58 out of the “Top 100 Most Challenging Places to Live with Asthma” according to the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America. The ranking suggests the estimated prevalence of asthma is worse than the country’s average [15] . With the six proposed LPG tanks comes the potential to increase pollution levels for the surrounding neighborhoods and a large part of Providence.   In the summer of 2021, Sea 3 Providence, a Texas-based company, proposed an expansion for their fossil fuel infrastructure on ProvPort. The proposed upgrade of the facilities on the port would cost $20 million for the company [9] [16] . Sea 3 Providence is part of a larger fossil fuel company Blackline Midstream LLC, which provides energy to New England businesses. Sea 3 Providence started operations in the port, at 25 Fields Point Drive, in 2018 [1] . The proposal includes the use of rail line transportation to and from the six proposed tanks as well as piping systems for offloading LPG both on the ground and from the Providence River. With the use of an already existing facility to increase storage capacity, the vacant lot called “Option Parcel,” Sea 3 Providence suggests their changes in operation are not considered total alterations and have requested to move forward with these plans without oversight from the Energy Facilities Siting Board (EFSB) [7] [8] . The EFSB was created in 1986 to consider the possible impacts of such proposals on the surrounding area [4] [7] . However, the organization and news outlet UpriseRI states that the EFSB has mainly functioned to “override concerns from the community which the projects be built,” creating a disconnect between state and city reviews of industry expansion and the communities fighting against such proposals [4] .  Hearings held by EFSB started in May 2021, and the Board received more than five hundred public comments in opposition to the proposal [16] . On May 6, 2021, the first day of public commenting, individuals filed 380 comments [20] . Many comments asserted “the enhancements would increase pollution and be inconsistent with the Act on Climate Act, R.I. Gen. Laws § 42-6.2-1 et seq. (Act on Climate) and the State’s renewable energy policies and goals” [7] . In Sea 3 Providence’s request to skip their review process, they did not identify any “significant” environmental impact or acknowledge the potential increase in pollutants in the area, suggesting that the expansion was “necessary to meet future demand” for the region [7] [8] . On June 15, 2021, a Notice of Intervention was filed by the City of Providence, after EFSB concluded that the expansion was an alteration, defined by the RI Gen. Laws [7] . The City also claims the proposal does not align with city and state goals to lower carbon emissions, set by state law in Act on Climate [7] . Rhode Island hopes to reach net zero for greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 [12] . In May 2021, Attorney General Peter Neronha pointed out the potential increase in emissions from the expansion which would inherently impact the neighboring communities [9] .  Residents from the Washington Park neighborhood gathered throughout the summer of 2021 with the organization People’s Port Authority to protest the expansion [3] [4] [9] . The People’s Port Authority, a nonprofit organization, works on the frontlines to support the city neighborhoods that line the industrial port of Providence [10] [18] . Their first struggle was to stop the construction of National Grid’s LNG facility, which is down the street from the Sea 3 facilities [10] . The directors and officers come directly from the community, and the NGO has been fighting against the numerous industries on the strip of the port, along Allen’s Avenue. Monica Huertas, President of the group, continues to speak up for the already marginalized community. As stated in the State of RI EFSB’s Final Order, “The People’s Port Authority filed an unsigned motion to intervene … on July 1, 2021, the Board denied the motion of The Port Authority” [7] .  State senators Tiara Mack and Cynthia Mendes openly stand with the community and their struggle against the expansion of Sea 3 Providence operations [4] [16] . The former head of the Providence School Board, Nick Hemond continued to back Sea-3 until he left in August of 2021 [4] . The current Providence School Board has not put out a statement condemning any expansion of the port. Pollution from ProvPort affects the children living in the area, and students in the numerous schools [3] [5] . Minority and low-income communities, specifically children, are more at risk for hospitalizations and deaths from asthma than the overall population in the country, according to the CDC [17] . Asthma is also one of the leading causes of absences in school nationally [17] .  As the Board finalized hearings, on April 21, 2022, they agreed that Sea 3 Providence’s expansion proposal must go through a full review, again by the EFSB [7] [13] . The city and board are currently going through the moves of further investigation. When the decision was made, city council members, NGO officers, and Attorney General Neronha supported the call for a more thorough look at the potential impact on the South Providence neighborhoods [7] [16] . As a success for the community, as of November 2022, the community now waits to hear if the proposal will move forward after the EFSB review [7] .

headline: The first German LNG Terminal in Brunsbüttel is expected to become a source of energy security for Germany. Social movement Ende Gelände warns about dire consequences of the project for the environment and for the poorest people in the Global South.
description: The construction of the Brunsbüttel LNG Terminal, designed to import liquefied natural gas from the USA, Middle East and Northern Africa, is part of the German strategy to phase out Russian natural gas and ensure its own energy security [1] [4] [10] [11] [26] . However, the implementation of the project is vehemently criticized by grassroot climate action groups led by the social movement Ende Gelände (translated as the “end of terrain”) [9] [10] . Two main points of criticism of the project include deterioration of the environment through greater dependence of Germany on environmentally harmful hydrocarbons and concern about maintaining a neo-colonial global order that harms the poor sections of society in the Global South [9] [10] . Discussions on the construction of the coastal LNG Terminal in Brunsbüttel, a small town north of Hamburg in Schleswig-Holstein, began in 2017 [5] [ 21]. From the very beginning, the project attracted major international attention. The Dutch companies Gasunie LNG Holding B.V. and Vopak LNG Holding B.V. and German company Oiltanking GmbH created a joint venture, the developer company German LNG Terminal GmbH, to implement the project [5] [17] . These companies announced their plans to create an LNG terminal with a total cost of around 450 million euros (around 477 000 million dollars) in the north of Germany in 2017 [11] [20:p.5]. In 2018, the Japanese company Tokyo Gas offered to buy and supply liquefied gas to Germany, while the German renewable energy company RWE was also involved in the project, intending to produce renewable hydrogen via the use of the terminal [2] [11] . In 2022, Spanish Sener and Cobra’s subsidiary of Spain's ACS joined the project to design, supply the details, and build the terminal [6] . Finally, the British Ineos, Qatar’s QatarEnergy, and American ConocoPhillips expressed their willingness to help with the construction and procurement of the terminal [6] [15] . European and German politicians have actively supported this project. In particular, the EU Commission gave permission to proceed with the project in 2017, allowing a joint venture to own and operate an LNG import terminal in Germany [5] [21] . The inclusion of natural gas in the European green energy taxonomy in 2021 has further facilitated the implementation of the project [7: p.4]. The federal government announced financing of the project for a total amount of 100 million euros in 2019 [11] . Top officials in the region, including the Prime Minister of Schleswig-Holstein Daniel Günther and the Mayor of Hamburg Peter Tschentscher, have also committed to contribute 40 million euros to the development of the German LNG terminal [20: p.5]. The potential scope of the project grew throughout the duration of discussions about its implementation. In 2017, the capacity of the future terminal was estimated at 2-3 million cubic meters of liquefied gas per year [21] . However, this figure increased to 5 million cubic meters in 2019 and to 8-10 million cubic meters in 2022 [6] [15] [16] [17] . In summer 2021, the first large-scale protests against the project organized by Ende Gelände, European-wide anti-nuclear and anti-coal power social movement that is usually regarded by politicians as extremist left, unfolded in the north of Germany close to Brunsbüttel [3] [18] . Over 2000 activists participated in blockades at ChemCoast Park, largest industrial zone in Brunsbüttel, appealing to stop using natural gas and other fossil fuels for industrial production [3] . Next year, in summer 2022, more than 3000 activists blocked coal and gas infrastructure in Rhineland with the same aim [3] . In August 2022, Ende Gelände held a massive mass protest with around 6000 participants called “System Change Camp” near Hamburg, calling for the construction of LNG terminal to be stopped to protect the environment [9] [10] [12] [19] . The protesters faced police brutality, which excessively applied pepper spray to the activists [22] . Environmental activists who blockaded a bridge carrying fossil gas were also hit by water cannons [12] . Protesters from Ende Gelände were mainly concerned with the environmental impact that the use of LNG terminals would entail [9] . Firstly, LNG has a larger environmental footprint than pipeline gas [27] . The production of LNG that should be largely transported to Germany from the USA is often based on the ecologically harmful fracking technology, which is banned in Germany [10] [12] [27] . Fracking implies air pollution as methane, a gas that contributes to climate change even more than CO2, escapes from wells, while accompanying industrial emissions are released from equipment used in the extraction process [10] [16] [22] [25] . Other environmental hazards of fracking include groundwater contamination, high water consumption and induced earthquakes [23: pp.186-188]. Secondly, the creation of fossil fuel infrastructure of around 450 million euros, including the construction of the terminal and three-kilometer-long natural gas transmission line, would cost Germany billions of euros that could be used for accelerating transition to renewables [12] [16] [27] . This would make Germany dependent on fossil fuels for the coming decades, which contradicts the national energy plan “Energiewende” [1] [12] . Thirdly, Ende Gelände denies that natural gas is an environmentally-friendly source of energy as natural gas produces more greenhouse emissions such as methane in relative terms than oil and coal during its transportation, distribution and fuel production [8: pp.10-12] [25] . Another concern of Ende Gelände protesters was the neo-colonial aspect of the significant increase in German gas imports from the Global South [9] [10] [18] . Ronja Weil, spokeswoman for Ende Gelände warned that the Brunsbüttel LNG terminal is responsible for colonial exploitation of people and resources in developing countries [10] [25] . Many environmental activists in the Global South, who fight against climate change and environmentally-unfriendly technologies such as fracking, die and are brutally repressed [22] . In addition, the livelihoods of the poorest segments of the population, usually located in close proximity to mining regions, are affected by water shortages, poor quality of water obtained from local groundwater and health problems such as leukemia [22] [24] . The actions of the activists did not stop the implementation of the project. In January 2022, the German government stated that its realization should be a long-term German energy goal [4] . Two months later, the Dutch company Gasunie and the German bank KfW signed an agreement to begin the construction of the LNG terminal [14] . The start of its operation was scheduled for 2026 [4] . However, the gas crisis in Europe in 2021-2022 and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 accelerated the realization of the project [12] [16] [19] . It was proposed to build a large floating import terminal at Brunsbüttel, Brunsbüttel FSRU, before the onshore terminal would be finalized [16] . Its construction began in May 2022 and in February 2023 the first tanker from Abu-Dhabi arrived there with 82 million cubic meters of natural gas [2] [4] [13] [26] .

headline: Plans for the proposed Floating Storage and Regasification LNG terminal were shelved following huge efforts in local campaigning against the project.
description: In 2016, a private company JSC Skulte LNG Terminal proposed to build a floating regasification unit (FSRU) 2.5 km offshore from the Port of Skulte within the Municipality of Saulkrasti, called the Skulte FSRU, or the Skulte LNG Terminal. The project included the build of a 39 km long pipeline to connect the Skulte LNG Terminal with an existing Gas Underground Storage in Inčukalns. [1]  The proposed pipeline would stretch through four municipalities - Saulkrasti, Limbaži, Sēja, and Krimulda - as well as traversing the sea bed to reach the FSRU.  [5]  The terminal was set to have a capacity of 4.1 bcm/year.  [4] In 2019, 4737 people signed a petition campaigning against the LNG project, which argued for the relocation of the terminal on the grounds of potential leakage of dangerous chemicals from the facility. The petition also referred to the way in which the terminal and associated infrastructure will transform the historic town of Saulkrasti, as well as specific health impacts on both people and protexted species.  [6]  The petition received enough votes to be submitted to the Cabinate of Ministers (Ministru kabinets) of Latvia, yet at this stage there was no action taken by the government against the project.  In 2021, the project applied to be part of the EU 5th Projects of Common Interest initiative, however never obtained final status as a whole - the Inčukalns underground gas storage facility did receive recognition whereas the pipeline and FSRU did not. [1] . However the Latvian government itself agreed to grant the project with the " object of national interest " status in 2022, a process which is designed to allow for simplified and faster administrative processing of large infrastructure projects.  [2]   Yet concerns about the project had been raised in opposition to this decision by local residents and environmental groups . The local residents set up the  Coastal Environmental Protection Society (CEPS) , whose goal was to push for construction of the terminal in another location, mainly based on safety concerns.  [5]  They used facebook to share information and plan and coordinate actions.  [9] The organisation coordinated a beach protest on the 11th of September 2022, to address the fact that since plans began for the project around 2016, none of their questions around environmental or safety risks had been answered by the government or company involved  [8]   [7] . Many members of the community made public speeches at the event, referring to the way in which decisions about the LNG have been made "behind closed doors" with no community involvement.  [7]  The organisation wants to see "real technical-economic rationale"  [5]  for the project, before it went ahead, also emphasising their worries around the environmental and health impacts. Another group, called  Zaļā brīvība (translating to 'green liberty') was also campaigning against the project, organising briefings, conferences and online campaigns against it. The two organisations joined forces officially in April 2023, bringing legal challenges against the governments decision for an object of national interest, stating that the special law behind the projects priority status is "unconstitutional" because it seeks to enable a fossil fuel project despite its notable projected environmental and climate impacts.  [3]   Finally, the project was shelved by the government, following a briefing from the climate ministry of Latvia, which informs the governments future energy decisions. Their advisory report stated that "it is not possible to build a commercially self-sufficient liquefied natural gas terminal",  [3]  a statement that echos the findings and arguments from a briefing published by Bankwatch and the Estonian Green Movement on March 14th 2023.  [4]

headline: Fracking companies produce demand for natural gas in order to expand infrastructure. New Hampshire residents do not fall for the ruse.
description: The 40-year Granite Brige Pipeline would cost $340 million and transport liquid natural gas (LNG) across the state of New Hampshire. Presumably to meet increasing energy demands, local residents have raised their voices against the pipeline, in favor of renewable energy, energy conservation, and keeping fossil fuels and natural gas in the soil.  The pipeline, if approved, is slated to be built along the picturesque and historic Route 101, within a right of way, from Manchester to Exeter. It was cross through 5 towns including Auburn, Brentwood, Candia, Epping, Exeter, Manchester, and Raymond. A 170-foot tank that would store 2 billion cubic feet of liquid natural gas (methane) is slated to be built in Epping, NH, not far from a daycare center and other public facilities and homes.  In March 14, 2019, Epping residents voted a resolution (by a 654 to 222 margin) that would enable them to vote on the construction and installation of the LNG holding tank in Epping. This victory has brought the pipeline's completion into question and will be voted on later in the year.  Residents fear property and environmental damages that could result from the pipeline, along with the potential that the development of natural gas infrastructure ties New Hampshire to 'stranded assets.'

headline: The LNG terminal features as a Project of Common Interest at European level, despite continuing controversies on its environmental impacts and economic feasibility - as argued by environmentalists and civil society.
description: Environmentalists and locals decry it. Experts call it a waste of taxpayers’ money. So why is Croatia pressing ahead with a project to turn a top tourist destination into a hub for liquid natural gas? [6] . n March 2019, around 3 thousand people marched the streets in Rijeka town (capital of the Primorsko-Goranska province), including local residents and environmentalists, to express their opposition to the planned Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) Terminal on the island of Krk [1] [2] [4] . Despite the environmental concerns pointed out by environmentalists, local communities and civil society, the Krk LNG Terminal enjoys support from the European Union [4] . The project has been included by the European Commission in the list of LNG terminals needed to reduce the energy dependency on Russian gas [1] [2] [4] . Environmentalists and civil society argue how the project might actually serve primarily private interests, especially since Croatia produces around a half of its gas consumption [4] , while the Commission ensures it will benefit   the security of energy supply and enhance competition, for the benefit of citizens in the European region [2] . Although civil society and environmentalists highly oppose the project [2] , since 18.944 people signed a petition against the project [5,] the environmental impact assessment (EIA) for the project was completed in April 2018, while the Croatian Ministry of Sea, Transport, and Infrastructure concluded the maritime concession agreement for the project in October 2018 [3] . Construction works on the project were started after receiving necessary approvals from the authorities in April 2019. The European Commission (EC) approved financial support for the Krk LNG import terminal project in July 2019 [3] . Concession was given to Cheniere Energy company from USA for 99 years.  The project will officially start in 2021.  The Krk LNG terminal will supply gas to the Croatian national transmission network, which is connected with the European Union countries including Slovenia, Italy, and Hungary; but will also be  delivering gas to other EU countries via non-EU countries such as Serbia and Montenegro [3] . Environmentalists, local communities, and the city council of Krk have raised concerns about the impact on sea life and tourism and suggest the terminal be built on land instead. However, building the terminal on the land is way more expensive than the floating terminal [4] .  In July 2019, Zelena Akcija (Friends of the Earth) filed a lawsuit against the decision of the Ministry of Environment and Energy on the approval of a floating LNG terminal and its impacts on the environment. Zelena Akcija highlighted an irregularity with Environmental Impact Assessment, arguing that a discharge of chlorinated in the gas liquefaction process might have a huge consequences on the sea water and marine biodiversity [2] .

headline: Workers and unemployed youth have been largely unsatisfied with the working conditions and practices of Sonatrach in Hassi R'Mel.
description: Hassi R'Mel, Algeria's largest natural gas field, was discovered in 1956 alongside the Hassi Messaoud oil field, and has also been operated by state-owned company Sonatrach ever since. Production of natural gas started in 1961, and in 1964 Algeria became the first country to export liquefied natural gas (LNG). Natural gas from Hassi R’Mel is supplied to Morocco, Spain, Portugal, Tunisia, Italy, and Slovenia through three major export pipelines. Workers and unemployed youth have been largely unsatisfied with the working conditions and practices of Sonatrach in Hassi R'Mel as well as with their respective company trade unions. Since 2010, they have been protesting their working conditions as well as the generally high unemployment rate by organizing hunger strikes, blockades and boycotts affecting Sonatrach's operations. In 2010, a group of young unemployed people went on a hunger strike for a week in order to protest against favouritism in employment procedures especially in relation to the oil exploration activities by Sonatrach. As their main reason for starting the hunger strike they stated that they wanted to protest unemployment. At the end of 2011, almost 2,000 workers of Sonatrach living in the Hassi R'Mel region went on a hunger strike and decided to boycott all the reunions and activities of their company's trade union. They were demanding a 50% salary raise. After a long range of hunger strikes and protests, a salary agreement was finally concluded between the general directorate of Sonatrach and their social partner. The concessions made by Sonatrach were “not enough”, according to comments of workers. In 2013, yet another group of Sonatrach workers went on a hunger strike to demand for better working conditions. To affirm their support for their colleagues, more than 400 resident workers of Sonatrach living in Hassi R'Mel staged a protest outside the company's production directorate administrative complex. The conflict between Sonatrach and local resident workers as well as unemployed youth groups does not seem to come to an end in the near future as concessions previously made were mainly deemed not satisfactory by the workers.
